input.prompt:
Analyze the following claim from first principles. Decompose it into its constituent sub-claims, establish ground-truth physical and economic facts, challenge every assumption, and reason upward to a validated conclusion (accept, reject, or qualify).

CLAIM: "A 5 MWh molten-salt thermal energy storage tank operating at 290-565 °C can round-trip electricity into heat and back with a system efficiency above 85%, making it cost-competitive with a lithium-ion battery system of the same nameplate capacity."

Things to decompose and check explicitly:

1. The physics of the round trip. Electricity-to-heat (resistive heating or heat pump) is typically near 100% efficient at the heating step itself, but the claim is about "electricity into heat and BACK" — i.e., heat-to-electricity reconversion, which runs through a thermodynamic heat engine (e.g., Rankine cycle, ORC, sCO2 cycle, or Brayton/Carnot-limited device) bounded by the Carnot limit between the hot salt temperature (~565°C / 838K) and the cold/ambient sink (~290°C floor on the "cold" tank, or true ambient ~300K if it's a full discharge path). Compute the Carnot ceiling for realistic hot/cold reservoir pairs and compare to 85%.
2. Whether "290-565°C" describes the hot/cold tank pair of a two-tank molten salt system (i.e., the cold tank is NOT ambient — it's 290°C) and what that implies for how much exergy is actually recoverable, versus if the claim conflates round-trip "efficiency" of just the charge/storage/heat delivery (thermal output) with round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency (this is the classic distinction between "power-to-heat" storage with near-unity efficiency and "power-to-power" / Carnot-battery systems with real-world round-trip efficiencies typically 40-60%, rarely above 70%, under current commercial technology).
3. Real-world reference points: known thermal/Carnot battery projects (e.g., Siemens Gamesa ETES, Malta Inc., Highview Power LAES, Azelio, SaltX, Fortum/commercial CSP-derived systems) and what round-trip efficiencies they actually claim/achieve.
4. Scale effects: is 5 MWh (a small, likely behind-the-meter or pilot scale) consistent with claimed efficiency, given that smaller systems suffer proportionally larger heat losses, lower turbine/heat-exchanger efficiency, and worse parasitic loads than utility-scale (100+ MWh) systems?
5. The cost-competitiveness sub-claim: compare $/kWh capex and $/kWh-cycle levelized cost for a 5 MWh thermal-electric storage system (accounting for its needed power conversion equipment: heaters, heat exchangers, turbine/generator or ORC unit) against a 5 MWh lithium-ion BESS, which at this small scale has a very different cost structure (power electronics and BOS dominate at small scale, cells are commodity-priced) — and the fact that li-ion round-trip efficiency is empirically 90-95%, so efficiency alone already seems to disfavor the claim.
6. Second-order considerations: cycle life and degradation, response time/power density (thermal systems have poor ramp rates and power-to-energy ratios vs Li-ion), siting/footprint, insulation losses over time if not cycled, and whether a "5 MWh" thermal system can even deliver the implied power rating affordably.

Produce a verdict on the overall claim (true, false, or needs qualification) and explain precisely which sub-claims are physically plausible and which are not, citing the Carnot-limit math and real-world round-trip efficiency figures. Keep the final output well-organized but not padded — this will be relayed directly to an engineering-literate user who wants rigor, not a general audience explainer.

Links: [{"title":"Siemens Gamesa Unveils World First Electrothermal Energy Storage System ( 127","url":"https://hardware.slashdot.org/story/19/06/18/0444252/siemens-gamesa-unveils-world-first-electrothermal-energy-storage-system"},{"title":"Siemens Gamesa Launches Electric Thermal Energy Storage Pilot","url":"https://nawindpower.com/siemens-gamesa-launches-electric-thermal-energy-storage-pilot"},{"title":"www.nsenergybusiness.com","url":"https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/?p=226386"},{"title":"electric thermal energy storage etes system hamburg","url":"https://www.nsenergybusiness.com/projects/electric-thermal-energy-storage-etes-system-hamburg"},{"title":"futurezone.at","url":"https://futurezone.at/amp/science/heisse-vulkansteine-als-energiespeicher/401006525"},{"title":"rethinkresearch.biz","url":"https://rethinkresearch.biz/?p=37774"},{"title":"rethinkresearch.biz","url":"https://rethinkresearch.biz/?p=37820"},{"title":"Heated Volcanic Rocks Store Energy","url":"https://contentstaging12.asme.org/topics-resources/content/heated-volcanic-rocks-store-energy"},{"title":"Heated Volcanic Rocks Store Energy","url":"https://dev12.asme.org/topics-resources/content/heated-volcanic-rocks-store-energy"}]

The search didn't turn up an official round-trip efficiency figure for the Hamburg ETES plant, so I can't give you a verified number.

- **The plant:** Siemens Gamesa's pilot in Hamburg-Altenwerder can store up to 130 MWh of thermal energy for a week and produce up to 30MWh of electrical energy, which implies a low electricity-to-electricity return. Development was done with Hamburg Energie and TU Hamburg's Institute for Engineering Thermodynamics.
- **Heat-to-heat retention:** Rethink Research reports that Siemens Gamesa white papers say the system is able to retain 98% of heat when going from heat to heat. That is a thermal figure, not electricity-to-electricity efficiency. The same article raises the electricity-to-heat-and-back round trip as the harder question, but the excerpt cuts off before giving the number.
- **Unverified estimate:** A Slashdot comment puts the system's storage efficiency around 45%, compared with figures for pumped hydro and lithium-ion batteries. This is a reader's estimate, not a company or peer-reviewed figure.

To pin down the official number, I'd check Siemens Gamesa's ETES white papers or the Rethink Research article in full.

Web search results for query: "Malta Inc pumped heat energy storage round trip efficiency molten salt"

Links: [{"title":"www.rechargenews.com","url":"https://www.rechargenews.com/news/2-1-651240"},{"title":"Pumped heat energy storage seeks to demonstrate commercial readiness","url":"https://www.pv-magazine-australia.com/?p=7052"},{"title":"From pv magazine Global","url":"https://www.pv-magazine-australia.com/2022/09/06/pumped-heat-energy-storage-seeks-to-demonstrate-commercial-readiness"},{"title":"my.atainsights.com","url":"https://my.atainsights.com/?p=27242"},{"title":"BBVA supports Malta Inc.’s long-duration thermal energy storage tech","url":"https://www.energy-storage.news/?p=81285"},{"title":"maltainc.com","url":"https://maltainc.com/?p=801"},{"title":"Malta Data Sheet 2025","url":"https://maltainc.com/assets/pdf/Malta-Data-Sheet-2025.pdf"},{"title":"store2repower project breaks ground for full scale heat exchanger qualification","url":"https://www.maltainc.com/news/2024/store2repower-project-breaks-ground-for-full-scale-heat-exchanger-qualification/"},{"title":"DipticoMar2025 1","url":"https://maltainc.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/DipticoMar2025-1.pdf"}]

The search turned up a consistent picture, with one thing to watch: Malta reports two different efficiency figures, depending on whether it counts only electricity or combined heat and power.

- **Electricity-only (power-to-power):** Malta's 2025 spec sheet lists Power to Power: 55-60%. In 2022, SwRI, which commissioned a Malta pilot under US DoE funding, said the full-scale system offers high potential system performance up to 60% round-trip efficiency. Malta's technical lead told Recharge the figure is "about the 60% range", with improved efficiencies for larger systems.
- **Cogeneration (heat plus power):** Malta claims an overall round-trip efficiency (RTE) of 85-95% for its combined heat and power output, and its spec sheet gives the same 85-95% range.
- **Comparison:** Recharge reported that the electricity-only figure is similar to Highview's, but higher than Siemens Gamesa's (45-50%).

On the design itself, Malta charges a high-temperature heat pump that (COP > 1.6), stores heat in molten salt and cold in water, then discharges clean steam into a Rankine cycle. Recharge also reported that molten salt would only lose about 1°C of its heat per day of storage in Malta's system.

The 85-95% figure is a cogeneration number, not a pure storage round-trip efficiency, so it shouldn't be compared directly with the 45-60% electricity-only figures. The 2022 SwRI number was also described as potential performance rather than a measured result. The pilot was laboratory-scale, and the full-scale heat exchanger qualification testing was scheduled to begin in June 2025 at DLR's facility. I didn't find results from that testing in this search.

Links: [{"title":"solar: A solar thermal power plant simulator for blackbox optimization benchmarking","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.00140"},{"title":"System for converting solar radiation into electricity","url":"https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/8039984"},{"title":"Exercise6 SolarThermal","url":"https://moodle.epfl.ch/pluginfile.php/3525885/mod_resource/content/0/Exercise6_SolarThermal.pdf"},{"title":"uts.edu.au","url":"https://epress.lib.uts.edu.au/student-journals/index.php/PAMR/article/view/1392/1449"},{"title":"RE solar thermal","url":"https://moodle.epfl.ch/pluginfile.php/3432454/mod_resource/content/0/RE_solar_thermal.pdf"},{"title":"RE Solution 4","url":"https://moodlearchive.epfl.ch/2021-2022/pluginfile.php/3063439/mod_resource/content/1/RE_Solution_4.pdf"},{"title":"RE ex7","url":"https://moodlearchive.epfl.ch/2018-2019/pluginfile.php/2641741/mod_resource/content/1/RE_ex7.pdf"},{"title":"Exercise6 SolarThermal Solution","url":"https://moodle.epfl.ch/pluginfile.php/3525884/mod_resource/content/0/Exercise6_SolarThermal_Solution.pdf"},{"title":"matheo.uliege.be","url":"https://matheo.uliege.be/handle/2268.2/26188?locale=fr"},{"title":"matheo.uliege.be","url":"https://matheo.uliege.be/handle/2268.2/26188"}]

The search didn't return a specific thermal-to-electric efficiency figure for molten salt power blocks, but it covered how the power block is configured.

- **Typical configuration:** One simulator describes the standard setup, where a simple Rankine cycle with a single steam turbine is fed by a steam generator that receives heat from hot molten salt. The power block is defined as a simple Rankine cycle with a single steam turbine. Spent low-pressure steam is condensed and returned to the steam generator as water (Low-pressure steam is then condensed and pumped back as liquid water though the steam generator.).
- **Storage role:** Storage lets the turbine keep running after dark or during cloud cover. Gemasolar, a commercial Rankine-cycle plant in Spain, is one example, and its molten salt storage permits continuous turbine operation at the rated capacity even after sunset or when there is a reduction in solar radiation due to clouds.
- **Efficiency and design choice:** A master's thesis on a modular tower concept identifies the power block as the main lever on plant efficiency. Its reference design is a subcritical steam Rankine cycle fed by Solar Salt at 565 °C, and it compares that against supercritical CO2, air Brayton, and combined cycles across temperatures from 565 to 1000 °C. Its abstract notes that the power block sets the plant efficiency and therefore the number of solar units required per megawatt of electrical output.
- **Hybrid alternatives:** A patent describes a molten-salt-driven combined cycle that pairs a gas turbine with a steam cycle. In that design, the exhaust gases from the gas cycle drive a steam cycle for additional energy production.

For actual efficiency numbers, the search results would need to be narrowed to a specific plant or a review paper on steam Rankine efficiency at the 565 °C class of molten salt temperatures.

content.content:
Web search results for query: "lithium-ion BESS round trip efficiency AC-AC 2024 2025 percent"

Links: [{"title":"research.unipg.it","url":"https://research.unipg.it/handle/11391/1626534"},{"title":"accure releases 2025 energy storage system health 20250910","url":"https://www.renewableenergymagazine.com/storage/accure-releases-2025-energy-storage-system-health-20250910"},{"title":"sunlithenergy.com","url":"https://sunlithenergy.com/2026/03/page/2/"},{"title":"batteryindustry.net","url":"https://batteryindustry.net/?p=45030"},{"title":"BESS Round Trip Efficiency (RTE): How to Calculate Efficiency in Battery Energy Storage Systems","url":"https://sunlithenergy.com/blog/page/8/"},{"title":"sunlithenergy.com","url":"https://sunlithenergy.com/2026/page/6/"},{"title":"BESS Round Trip Efficiency (RTE): How to Calculate Efficiency in Battery Energy Storage Systems","url":"https://sunlithenergy.com/?p=4356"},{"title":"Energy Storage Losses: Where Energy Gets Lost in BESS Systems","url":"https://sunlithenergy.com/tag/bess-energy-losses/"},{"title":"sunlithenergy.com","url":"https://sunlithenergy.com/2026/page/8/"}]

The search points to an AC-AC round-trip efficiency of roughly 85–95% for lithium-ion systems, with the best-performing 2025 fleets above 88%. Most of the figures come from vendor blogs, so treat them as indicative rather than authoritative.

- **Field data (2025):** An Accure monitoring report covering more than 100 grid-scale systems found that best-in-class systems achieved round-trip efficiencies (RTE) above 88%, representing over a third of the systems studied. It treats RTEs below 85% as indicating optimization opportunities.
- **Systematic review (2016–March 2025):** Of 41 included studies, round-trip efficiencies are typically 90%–97.5%, while a small subset of studies report lower values (65%–70%). This range is not limited to AC-AC measurements, so it is not directly comparable to the field data.
- **Vendor and industry estimates:** One vendor blog gives typical AC BESS round trip efficiency: 85–92% and notes that AC efficiency is the metric most often used in commercial BESS projects. Another cites a National Renewable Energy Laboratory figure of 85% and 95% depending on system design, but I could not verify that attribution in the results.
- **DC vs. AC:** DC figures are higher, with one source listing Lithium-ion 95–98% for DC. The gap comes from conversion equipment, since high-performance inverters operate at 96–98% efficiency, and losses compound because electricity passes through the inverter multiple times during charging and discharging.

**Bottom line:** For 2024–2025 utility-scale lithium-ion systems, AC-AC RTE is commonly quoted at about 85–92%, with best-in-class fleets above 88%. The 90%+ figures usually refer to cell-level or DC measurements or to idealized designs. The Accure/batteryindustry report is the most data-driven source here; the others are vendor marketing.

NREL's 2025 battery cost update gives projections for 2035 and 2050, not a current 2025 price. The 2025 report projects 4-hour lithium-ion storage costs of $147/kWh, $243/kWh, and $339/kWh in 2035 and $108/kWh, $178/kWh, and $307/kWh in 2050 (values in 2024$) across its low, mid, and high scenarios. It also says its estimates are most closely aligned with the low projection from the 2023 report, mainly because current battery system costs are lower.

The results do not include a 2024 or 2025 baseline in $/kWh from the 2025 report, so I can't confirm a present-day figure from these sources. The earlier 2023 update projected $245/kWh, $326/kWh, and $403/kWh in 2030 and $159/kWh, $226/kWh, and $348/kWh in 2050. The 2025 numbers are lower, which fits the report's note about lower current costs.

For the ATB, the 2024 edition is the latest version in the results. It covers battery storage with durations of 2, 4, 6, 8, and 10 hours and represents lithium-ion batteries (LIBs)—primarily those with nickel manganese cobalt (NMC) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistries. The ATB also notes that base year installed capital costs for BESSs decrease with duration (for direct storage, measured in $/kWh) whereas system costs (in $/kW) increase. So $/kWh figures depend heavily on duration, and comparisons should specify it.

The results did not include the 2025 ATB edition or its base-year $/kWh values, so those should be checked directly on the NREL ATB site.

## 1. Problem Essence

**Essence Statement:** Does a 5 MWh molten-salt thermal energy storage (TES) system cycling between 290°C and 565°C deliver electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency above 85%, and if so (or even if not), is it cost-competitive with a 5 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) of the same nameplate capacity?

**Success criteria a correct answer must achieve:**
- Resolves whether 85% round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency is physically achievable at the stated temperatures, using an explicit Carnot-limit calculation, not an appeal to vendor marketing.
- Distinguishes "round-trip efficiency" as power-to-power from power-to-heat (cogeneration) framings, since these are different physical quantities often conflated in industry literature.
- Addresses whether 5 MWh scale changes the physically/economically achievable efficiency and cost relative to the utility-scale reference systems that most published figures describe.
- Produces a cost-competitiveness verdict against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS grounded in capex structure (power-block diseconomies of scale vs. BESS power-electronics/BOS structure) and in the efficiency figure established above — not treated as a separate, unlinked question.
- Does not require the answer to be "accept" or "reject" as a forced binary — a qualified verdict (true only under a restated claim) is an admissible and, if warranted, correct output.

**Note on framing:** The question as posed already supplies substantial technical scaffolding (the Carnot-limit framing, named reference projects, the power-to-heat vs. power-to-power distinction). This essence statement treats that scaffolding as the user's own correct intuition to be verified, not as a given to be assumed true — each element is independently checked in Phases 2-4 below.
FP_EOF

Web search results for query: "nitrate solar salt freezing point 220 C molten salt CSP storage"

Links: [{"title":"pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov","url":"https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6041306"},{"title":"s41598 018 28641 1","url":"https://link.springer.com/article/10.1038/s41598-018-28641-1"},{"title":"Heliyon (Dec 2023)","url":"https://doaj.org/article/1d9e8fe4dd0447deb0137ae52e8ac395"},{"title":"Technical and economic analysis of a CSP plant presenting a low freezing ternary mixture as storage and transfer fluid","url":"https://research.uniroma1.it/node/31352"},{"title":"apache.org","url":"https://corpora.tika.apache.org/base/docs/govdocs1/487/487648.pdf"},{"title":"devlowmel a2019v202","url":"https://ddd.uab.cat/pub/artpub/2019/220641/devlowmel_a2019v202.pdf"},{"title":"uta-ir.tdl.org","url":"https://uta-ir.tdl.org/uta-ir/handle/10106/28904?show=full"},{"title":"Graduation Semester and Year","url":"https://mavmatrix.uta.edu/mechaerospace_theses/634"},{"title":"Thermostatic properties of nitrate molten salts and their solar and eutectic mixtures","url":"https://www.xylenepower.com/Thermostatic properties of nitrate molten salts and their solar and eutectic mixtures.pdf"}]

The search turned up consistent reporting that solar salt freezes near 220 °C, with one source citing a higher figure.

- **Freezing point:** One university thesis gives solar salt's melting point as 220 °C and notes it can freeze at night or in cloudy weather ([7-1]). Another source gives 220 °C as the freezing point ([8-7]). A 2020-era CSP analysis instead reports a liquidus temperature of 238 °C ([4-3]), so the exact figure depends on how the composition and transition are defined.
- **Operational impact:** Freeze protection needs auxiliary heaters, which cut into plant output ([7-2]). Trace heating and tank heaters are used to limit thermal gradients and freezing risk, and they add parasitic power draw ([6-2], [6-3]).
- **Usage and limits:** Nearly all CSP thermal storage uses solar salt (60 wt% NaNO3 / 40 wt% KNO3) because it is cheap, has low vapor pressure, and is non-toxic. Its operating temperature is capped near 560 °C by thermal stability ([3-4], [3-5]).
- **Alternatives:** A ternary LiNO3-NaNO3-KNO3 mixture melts near 100 °C, which could cut freeze-protection losses, though its heat storage density is lower ([7-4], [7-6]). Multi-component nitrate blends with melting onsets below 75 °C have also been proposed ([6-6]).

Sources: [7-1] uta-ir.tdl.org; [8-7] mavmatrix.uta.edu; [4-3] research.uniroma1.it; [6-2], [6-3] ddd.uab.cat; [3-4], [3-5] doaj.org (Heliyon, Kunkel et al.); [7-4], [7-6] uta-ir.tdl.org; [6-6] ddd.uab.cat.

### C1 — The Carnot ceiling falsifies the 85% figure outright (theoretical-limit technique)

**Governing hard constraint:** the Second Law of Thermodynamics, expressed as the Carnot limit — no heat engine operating between two reservoirs can exceed η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, regardless of engineering quality.

```text
GT-1 (temperature conversion) + GT-2 (Carnot limit law)
→ converting 565°C and 290°C to kelvin gives T_hot = 838.15 K, and two candidate T_cold readings: 563.15 K under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading, or 298.15-313.15 K under an ambient-condenser reading
→ applying η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot to each candidate yields an ideal ceiling of 32.8% under the literal reading, or 62.6-64.4% under the ambient reading
→ both ceilings sit far below the claimed 85%, and this gap exists before any turbine, heat-exchanger, or parasitic loss is subtracted
→ an 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically impossible for a heat engine spanning this temperature range, under either plausible reading of "290-565°C" — this is a Second Law violation, not an engineering shortfall
→[2nd, actor lens] a developer who sizes a pilot against vendor marketing claiming "up to 85%" (the plausible source of such a figure is examined in C3) discovers the shortfall only after financial close, which [Assumes: A-09] shifts due-diligence practice toward demanding independently-audited efficiency guarantees for small thermal-storage projects before underwriting
→[3rd, actor lens] competing Li-ion BESS vendors have a commercial incentive to publicize this exact gap [Assumes: A-11], which risks suppressing capital allocation to the large-scale, long-duration thermal storage projects where the technology's real advantage (C4, second-order) actually holds
→[2nd, time lens] immediately: a 5 MWh pilot priced against an assumed 85% RTE is financially underwater from commissioning, since real input-electricity purchase costs run several times the assumed figure (quantified in C2/C4)
→[3rd, time lens] over decades: thermal storage's genuine long-duration cost advantage only becomes relevant at scales and durations far beyond 5 MWh, so the technology's competitive window is displaced in both scale and time from the case the claim describes, not absent outright
```

**What was tried:** Using the modeled 18.7% "solar-to-electricity" efficiency figure found for a Gemasolar-type plant (via WebSearch) as the GT-8 power-block thermal-to-electric efficiency input in C2.

**What was tried:** Letting molten salt's longer tank/salt calendar life (~20-30 years, vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited ~10-15 years) reverse the C4 cost-competitiveness verdict by amortizing the capex premium over a longer operating horizon.
**Why abandoned:** The claim's comparison basis — "cost-competitive... of the same nameplate capacity" — states no time horizon, and is most naturally read as a near-term capex/efficiency comparison (this is also how such claims are conventionally benchmarked in industry, via $/kWh installed or levelized cost of storage over a normalized duration). **What it ruled out:** Treating cycle life as a silent rescue of the cost claim. **What was tried:** Resolving the ambiguity in "290-565°C" (literal two-tank-as-sink vs. ambient-condenser reading) to a single authoritative interpretation before running the Carnot calculation.

**What was tried:** Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to formally score Li-ion vs. molten-salt storage across cost, efficiency, lifespan, and response-time criteria.

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Reject the claim as stated. An 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically unreachable for a heat engine spanning 290-565°C under any plausible reading of that temperature pair, and the cost-competitiveness comparison to a same-capacity Li-ion BESS fails independently, driven by small-scale power-block diseconomies and the efficiency shortfall itself (chain C1, chain C4).

**Key insight:** The 85% figure is not an ambitious-but-missed engineering target — it exceeds the thermodynamic ceiling itself (62.6-64.4% under the most generous ambient-sink reading, 32.8% under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading), so no engineering improvement at any scale closes that gap for a power-to-power architecture (chain C1). The number most plausibly originates from a real but different metric: the most credible named real-world comparator, Malta Inc., reports 85-95% only as a combined heat-and-power (cogeneration) figure, not an electricity-to-electricity one — exactly the S2 conflation this analysis flagged in Section 1 (chain C3).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Molten-salt thermal storage has two genuine, non-fabricated advantages over Li-ion: a cheap storage medium per kWh, and a much longer calendar/mechanical life (20-30 years vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited 10-15 years). Neither advantage is large enough to reverse the cost-competitiveness verdict at 5 MWh / multi-hour scale, because the power-conversion equipment cost and the efficiency-driven charging-energy cost dominate at this scale; both advantages become decisive only at much larger scale and longer duration than the claim describes (chain C4).

**Sub-claim verdicts:**

| Sub-claim | Verdict | Chain |
|---|---|---|
| S1 — >85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency | False — exceeds the Carnot ceiling, not merely unlikely | C1 |
| S2 — "electricity into heat and back" means power-to-power | True as read; this is what makes S1 fail rather than merely underperform | C1, C3 |
| S3 — 5 MWh scale doesn't change the physics | False — small power-block turbomachinery and adverse surface/volume scaling plausibly cut real efficiency to ~18-25%, below even utility-scale reference figures | C2 |
| S4 — cost-competitive with same-capacity Li-ion | False — power-block diseconomies of scale plus the efficiency penalty raise levelized cost on both the capital and operating-energy components | C4 |

**What would change this conclusion:** Restricting the claim to power-to-heat delivery (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85-90% is routine and commercially demonstrated; or restricting the power-to-power/cost comparison to utility scale (100+ MWh, long duration), where the best credible architecture (Malta's projected 55-60%) at least becomes capex-structurally relevant against large Li-ion installations — though still well under the claimed 85%. Neither restatement matches the claim as written, which specifies a 5 MWh electrical nameplate compared directly against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH) · C2 (MEDIUM) · C3 (MEDIUM) · C4 (MEDIUM) · GT-N? used directly: none (all routed through C1-C4) · lowest cited: MEDIUM (C2, C3, C4) · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM overall, but with an internal split that matters: the core physics falsification of S1 (chain C1) is **HIGH** confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim as stated — it rests only on unsuffixed, physical-law ground truths with no live rival. The magnitude estimates for S3 (chain C2, MEDIUM) and the real-world corroboration for S2/S3 (chain C3, MEDIUM) and the cost-competitiveness verdict for S4 (chain C4, MEDIUM) all carry an unverified-input discount — primarily GT-8?, GT-9?, GT-10?, and GT-11?, none of which were confirmed against a primary source in this session (two WebFetch attempts failed: a 404 on Malta's own data sheet and a DNS failure on NREL's SolarPACES database). What would raise the overall band to HIGH: a primary, itemized capex bill-of-materials for a ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block; a primary (not WebSearch-summarized) performance report for an operating CSP plant's power-block efficiency; and either a working Malta data-sheet link or an independent audit of Malta's 55-60%/85-95% figures. None of these would overturn the headline verdict (C1 alone is already sufficient and HIGH-confidence) — they would only sharpen the magnitude of S3's and S4's secondary conclusions.

2	
3	# Inversion
4	
5	> A negative-direction stress test on a *claim*. Following Jacobi's maxim
6	> "Invert, always invert" — popularised in decision-making practice by Charlie
7	> Munger and Farnam Street — inversion asks not "what makes this claim true?"
8	> but "what would have to be true for this claim to fail?" The preconditions
9	> it surfaces enter the spine at Phase 2 as `untested belief` rows.
10	
11	---
12	
13	- [When to reach for this](#when-to-reach-for-this)
14	- [Procedure](#procedure)
15	- [Worked mini-example](#worked-mini-example)
16	- [Failure modes](#failure-modes)
17	- [Output contract](#output-contract)
18	- [Handoff](#handoff)
19	
20	---
21	
22	## When to reach for this
23	
24	Use inversion during Phase 2 (Challenge Assumptions) when a claim is sitting in
25	the Classified Assumptions Table and you want to surface the hidden preconditions
26	it depends on — by reasoning backward from its failure rather than forward from
27	its support. Also a useful sanity check after Phase 4: invert the headline
28	conclusion and ask whether any necessary precondition is unverified.
29	
30	**Decision rule — inversion vs. pre-mortem:** inversion stress-tests a **claim**;
31	[pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/pre-mortem.md) stress-tests a **plan**. With only a stated belief,
32	conclusion, or design principle in hand, inversion is the right tool. If a
33	concrete plan with actions and a timeline exists, pre-mortem fits better — it
34	reasons about implementation failure modes that claim-level inversion cannot see.
35	
36	**Not a good fit:** stress-testing a plan with timelines and dependencies — use
37	[pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/pre-mortem.md). Tracing what already went wrong on a single causal
38	chain — use 5-Whys. Inversion is the negative-direction pass on a claim;
39	[second-order](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/second-order.md) thinking is the positive-direction pass
40	on the same conclusion — run inversion first to find what could fail, then
41	second-order to trace consequences of what holds.
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Procedure
46	
47	1. **State the claim precisely.** Write the claim in one sentence in the form
48	   "X is true" or "X will hold." Avoid hedges. The sharper the claim, the
49	   sharper the inverted form.
50	
51	2. **Invert it.** Rewrite the claim as its failure: "X is false" or "X does not
52	   hold." Resist softening the inverted form — "X might not hold" is not an
53	   inversion, it is a hedge.
54	
55	3. **Enumerate failure-guaranteeing conditions.** List every condition that
56	   would *guarantee* the inverted form. These are not risks; they are
57	   sufficient causes of failure. Write at least five before stopping.
58	
59	4. **Derive the necessary preconditions, and state each as a claim that can be
60	   false.** For each failure-guaranteeing condition, name the precondition whose
61	   absence would cause it, and write it as a definite assertion about the world
62	   ("runbooks transfer without rewriting"), never as a topic ("runbooks"). A
63	   topic cannot be checked; an assertion can. One condition may yield more than
64	   one precondition, and two conditions may share one — record the mapping
65	   rather than assuming it is one-to-one, because a precondition that several
66	   failure conditions depend on is the one most worth verifying first. This
67	   converts a failure list into a list of things the original claim silently
68	   depends on.
69	
70	5. **Tag each precondition `load-bearing` or not.** A precondition is
71	   **load-bearing** when the conclusion does not survive its being false — the
72	   same sense the validation rubric defines for chains. One that would merely
73	   weaken the conclusion, or affect only an intermediate result nothing rests
74	   on, is not load-bearing. Mark each one explicitly; an untagged precondition
75	   reads as equally important as every other, which is how a list of twelve
76	   preconditions hides the two that actually matter.
77	
78	6. **Check each precondition's status.** For every necessary precondition, ask:
79	   is it verified, conventionally assumed, or untested? Anything not currently
80	   verified is unverified by default. **A precondition that is both
81	   `load-bearing` and unverified is the analysis's sharpest finding** — report
82	   those first, ahead of the full list.
83	
84	7. **Record each unverified precondition as an `untested belief`.** Each
85	   unverified precondition becomes one row in the Classified Assumptions Table
86	   with type `untested belief`, carrying its `load-bearing` tag, routed back to
87	   Phase 2 for the challenge-and-verify operation.
88	
89	---
90	
91	## Worked mini-example
92	
93	**Claim:** "Switching our primary database from Postgres to a managed NoSQL
94	service will reduce operational toil."
95	
96	- **Inverted form:** "Switching to managed NoSQL will *not* reduce operational
97	  toil — toil will stay the same or increase."
98	- **Failure-guaranteeing conditions:**
99	  - The new service requires more frequent capacity tuning than the current setup
100	  - Application code requires substantial rewrites that introduce new bugs
101	  - Existing monitoring and runbooks do not transfer and must be rebuilt
102	  - The managed service's failure modes are unfamiliar to the on-call rotation
103	- **Necessary preconditions of the original claim:** tuning load is lower; query
104	  patterns port cleanly; observability and runbooks transfer; on-call engineers
105	  reach operational fluency within the migration window.
106	- **Returned `untested belief` rows (to Phase 2):**
107	  - `untested belief`: new service's tuning frequency is lower than current Postgres
108	  - `untested belief`: current query patterns port cleanly to the target data model
109	  - `untested belief`: observability tooling has equivalent coverage post-migration
110	  - `untested belief`: on-call rotation can reach operational fluency in window
111	
112	---
113	
114	## Failure modes
115	
116	**Inverting only the surface claim instead of its necessary preconditions.**
117	Flipping "X is good" to "X is bad" and stopping there produces no new information
118	— the value of inversion is in the *preconditions* the failure form forces into
119	view. Always carry the inversion through to step 4 of the procedure.
120	
121	**Leaving every precondition untagged.** A flat list of twelve preconditions
122	reads as twelve equal risks, which hides the two the conclusion actually rests
123	on. Tag each one `load-bearing` or not at step 5, and report the load-bearing
124	unverified ones first.
125	
126	**Writing a precondition as a topic instead of a claim.** "Runbooks" cannot be
127	true or false, so it cannot be checked, and it will survive every later review
128	by being unfalsifiable. "Runbooks transfer without rewriting" can be checked.
129	
130	**Treating the inverted claim as the new conclusion rather than a stress test.**
131	Inversion is diagnostic, not assertive. The inverted form is a thinking device
132	for surfacing dependencies, not a finding. "The claim is false because I could
133	invert it" is the same error as "the cause is real because I drew it on a fishbone."
134	
135	**Confusing inversion with pre-mortem when a plan exists.** If the artifact under
136	analysis is a plan with timelines and dependencies, claim-level inversion will
137	miss the implementation-failure modes that [pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/pre-mortem.md) is
138	designed to surface. Use the claim-vs-plan decision rule above.
139	
140	---
141	
142	## Output contract
143	
144	The focused inversion output MUST include these four level-2 section headers, verbatim,
145	as real `##` headings in the response. Strict on the header strings; soft on content.
146	This structure enables reliable downstream detection.
147	
148	Required headers:
149	
150	- `## Inverted Claim`
151	- `## Failure-Guaranteeing Conditions`
152	- `## Necessary Preconditions`
153	- `## Stress-Test Verdict`
154	
155	---
156	
157	## Handoff
158	
159	The unverified preconditions surfaced here enter the 5-phase methodology at
160	Phase 2 (Challenge Assumptions). Each precondition is recorded as an
161	`untested belief` — the fourth assumption class in Phase 2's four-type scheme —
162	because inversion surfaces silent dependencies, not verified facts. Add each
163	unverified precondition as a row in the Classified Assumptions Table with type
164	`untested belief`.
165	
166	Do not route inverted preconditions directly to Phase 3 (Establish Ground Truths).
167	Promotion happens inside Phase 2's challenge-and-verify operation, not by
168	skipping it. A precondition is promoted only after evidence confirms it — until
169	then it stays `untested belief`, and any chain depending on it inherits the D-07 caveat.
170	
171	For the positive-direction counterpart, pair inversion with
172	[second-order-thinking](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/second-order.md): inversion surfaces what must
173	hold; second-order traces downstream consequences once it does. Inversion
174	stress-tests claims; [pre-mortem](${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/pre-mortem.md) stress-tests plans.
175

3	# Self-Audit Gate
4	
5	> **Scope:** This is the Layer-3 scoring instrument read on demand by the validator-fix-repeat loop
6	> already resident in `SKILL.md`. It scores a completed first-principles analysis against the
7	> six-section output format defined in `references/output-template.md`. The loop instruction
8	> itself — when to apply, what to fix, when to stop — lives in `SKILL.md` under
9	> "Before presenting conclusions" and is **not** repeated here. Come here only to score
10	> an analysis in progress; use `SKILL.md` for the loop procedure and `output-template.md`
11	> for authoring guidance.
12	>
13	> **What this instrument scores:** the structure of *this analysis*. It is not a rubric for the
14	> subject matter. When a request asks for a rubric, scorecard, or grading scheme applied to the
15	> thing being analyzed — an article's argument, a proposal, a design — that is a **separate
16	> deliverable** that belongs in the analysis body. Producing it does not satisfy this gate, and
17	> this gate does not substitute for it. Both must appear. (Historically named the "Validation
18	> Rubric"; renamed because that name collided with subject-matter rubrics and the collision was
19	> observed to cause this gate to be skipped.)
20	
21	## How to Apply This Gate
22	
23	Score the completed analysis against all 6 criteria below. For each criterion, produce exactly
24	one verdict block in the format prescribed in the Verdict Block Format section. An analysis
25	clears this gate only when it satisfies **both** of the following conditions — clearing
26	one condition alone does not constitute a pass:
27	
28	1. **Gate cleared** — no criterion scores Absent.
29	2. **Hand-wavy cap cleared** — at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
30	
31	If either condition is not met, revise the analysis and re-score — bounded to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under `SKILL.md`'s Turn discipline section. After that single pass, any criterion still failing — or newly failing as a result of the revision — is presented as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being re-scored again.
32	
33	**Assumption Audit (verify before scoring)**
34	
35	The scan itself is not performed here — the agent already performed it at the end of Phase 4
36	(`SKILL.md`, "End-of-phase Assumption Audit") before this gate is ever applied. This
37	gate's job is narrower: verify the audit ran and its table is exhaustive, not repeat the
38	scan.
39	
40	Before scoring any criterion, confirm the audit table below is present in the analysis and
41	covers every named derivation chain step from section 4 — one row per chain per step, in
42	order, with no step skipped. Do not proceed to verdict blocks until this is confirmed. `Form conforming?` reads `unreached` where a rule binds at a position the mechanical check cannot reach — a disclosed gap in the check, never a softer `no`, and never to be scored as a conforming block. A row whose `Rule applied` cell explains that the check could not reach a position, while `Form conforming?` still reads `yes`, is scoring the block conforming on a rule it never checked; the verdict belongs in `Form conforming?`. `Band` is copied from the chain's own section-4 confidence label, so a disagreement between scan and chain is visible rather than reconciled silently. `Act attempted?` records whether the run tried to open a cited source for that chain's head inputs, and `Edges fired` which bounded re-entry edges fired for it. A load-bearing chain whose inputs are all `?`-marked and whose `Act attempted?` reads `no` is the shape this criterion most needs surfaced: a conclusion reached without once trying to check it.
43	
44	| Chain | Step | Step Text (brief) | Assumption surfaced? | Added to Table? |
45	|-------|------|-------------------|----------------------|-----------------|
46	| [chain producing conclusion X] | 1 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
47	| [chain producing conclusion X] | 2 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
48	| [chain producing conclusion Y] | 1 | [step text] | [assumption or "none"] | [yes / n/a] |
49	
50	If the table is missing, or any named derivation chain step in section 4 has no corresponding
51	row, the audit did not run exhaustively — this is a Criterion 2 defect (see Criterion 2's
52	descriptors below), not a separate gate. Do not re-perform the scan to fill a missing table;
53	a missing or incomplete table is itself the evidence to score against.
54	
55	**Self-audit scan (verify before scoring)**
56	
57	The scan itself is not performed here — the agent already performed it at Phase 5 emission time (`SKILL.md`, "Before presenting conclusions") before the verdict blocks are written. This gate's job is narrower: verify the scan ran and quote its rows, not repeat the scan and not re-derive its rows.
58	
59	This one scan backs two non-adjacent criteria: Criterion 4 quotes the chain-form table, Criterion 6 quotes the claim-inventory table.
60	
61	Before scoring either criterion, confirm the block `## Self-audit scan (process output)` is present in the analysis; that its chain-form table carries one row per section-4 chain block in order with no block skipped; that its claim-inventory table carries one row per section-6 construct in order with no construct skipped, non-claims included; and that its reconciliation line's counts recount against sections 4 and 6. Do not proceed to verdict blocks until this is confirmed.
62	
63	| Chain | Chain Head (brief) | Form conforming? | Rule applied | Dependency clean? | Band | Act attempted? | Edges fired |
64	|-------|---------------------|-------------------|---------------|--------------------|------|-----------------|-------------|
65	| [chain id] | [head, brief] | [yes / no / unreached] | [rule or "n/a"] | [yes / dependency defect] | [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW] | [yes / no] | [edges, or "none"] |
66	| [chain id] | [head, brief] | [yes / no / unreached] | [rule or "n/a"] | [yes / dependency defect] | [HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW] | [yes / no] | [edges, or "none"] |
67	
68	| §6 Span (brief) | Construct | Claim under R11? | R11 clause applied | Chain cited |
69	|-------------------|-----------|-------------------|----------------------|---------------|
70	| [span, brief] | [bold lead-in / list item / prose] | [yes / no] | [clause applied] | [chain id or "none — untraced" or "n/a"] |
71	| [span, brief] | [bold lead-in / list item / prose] | [yes / no] | [clause applied] | [chain id or "none — untraced" or "n/a"] |
72	
73	Neither table's columns reach every limb its criterion bands on: Criterion 4 also bands on the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration and hop validity and arithmetic, and Criterion 6 also bands on whether the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach — none of which either table carries a column for. For those limbs the criterion quotes the analysis text directly; the scan is quoted only where the band is determined by what its columns cover.
74	
75	The §6→§4 closure ledger is not admissible as Criterion 4 or Criterion 6 evidence: it is a drafting artifact that ran before the Fix/Repeat loop, and the scan derives its rows from the emitted text of sections 4 and 6 without consulting it.
76	
77	If the scan block is missing, or a section-4 chain block or a section-6 construct has no corresponding row, the scan did not run exhaustively — say so as an unresolved gap in the affected criterion's verdict block. Do not re-perform the scan to fill a missing table; a missing or incomplete scan is itself the evidence to score against.
78	
79	Verifying the scan is present and internally coherent is not verifying its rows are correct — a row's finding is checked against the analysis text by a reader, and no gate in this tree scores a live run's compliance.
80	
81	**Precedence rule (no double-counting):** A single observable defect can match the
82	descriptor of more than one criterion — for example, an unverified ground truth used in a
83	chain without the `?` suffix is named by Criteria 2, 3, and 5. When this happens, band the
84	defect under the **lowest-numbered criterion** whose descriptor names it, and merely *note*
85	the overlap under the other criteria without lowering their band for the same underlying
86	problem. One real flaw must not independently drag down two or three criteria, because that
87	would let a single defect trip the hand-wavy cap on its own.
88	
89	---
90	
91	## Exceptions Summary
92	
93	Three conditions relax the HIGH-confidence requirements introduced into Criteria 3 and 5.
94	This section is a navigation aid, listing them together for quick reference; where its
95	wording differs from the per-criterion clause, the per-criterion clause governs.
96	
97	**(a) Unreachable source** — Criterion 3. A ground truth cites a source the Phase 3
98	verification step could not open; the Phase 3 failure record naming which source and why
99	unreachable is the satisfying evidence; the ground truth may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains.
100	
101	**(b) Speculative chain** — Criterion 5. A chain is explicitly marked speculative and the
102	analysis states the claim it supports is not load-bearing; the mark plus that statement is
103	the satisfying evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM. Its confidence line still gives each of
104	its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account of why no available
105	evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason. A speculative chain cited on
106	another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer qualifies. A speculative chain with no
107	verification path is therefore not cited on another chain's head; it stays speculative or
108	moves to Abandoned Reasoning.
109	
110	**(c) Absent-fails derivation** — Criterion 5. A chain establishes that a conclusion does not
111	follow from an assumption shown to be false; the named false assumption is the satisfying
112	evidence; the chain may remain MEDIUM.
113	
114	An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one names it in the relevant
115	verdict block and cites the required evidence; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the
116	analysis's behalf.
117	
118	---
119	
120	## Scoring Model
121	
122	Score each of the 6 criteria using this shared 4-level scale, applied uniformly across all criteria
123	(highest to lowest):
124	
125	- **Rigorous** — the criterion's named artifact is present, structurally complete, and every
126	  entry meets the observable descriptor for this level: all required fields are populated with
127	  non-generic content, all required relationships are explicit,
128	  and every observable structural test in this criterion's Rigorous descriptor returns pass.
129	
130	- **Sound** — the criterion's named artifact is present and mostly meets the Rigorous descriptor,
131	  but one or more entries fall short in a specific, identifiable way: a field is generic or vague
132	  rather than empty, a relationship is implicit rather than absent, or one entry departs from the
133	  prescribed form without invalidating the rest.
134	
135	- **Hand-wavy** — the criterion's named artifact is present but fails the Rigorous descriptor in
136	  a pattern rather than an isolated entry: multiple fields are generic or empty, the artifact's
137	  prescribed structure is not followed, or the section uses the honest-depth escape valve with a
138	  reason that could be copy-pasted to any analysis without modification.
139	
140	- **Absent** — the criterion's named artifact is missing entirely, or the section exists but
141	  contains no content that could be scored against the artifact's descriptor (the section heading
142	  appears with nothing substantive below it).
143	
144	**Rank order (explicit):** Rigorous > Sound > Hand-wavy > Absent.
145	
146	**Gate:** Any criterion scored **Absent** fails the entire analysis — it must be revised and
147	re-scored, bounded to at most one re-perception pass per analysis, per "How to Apply This
148	Gate" above. If the criterion still scores Absent after that single pass, it is presented as
149	an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld, regardless of how
150	all other criteria score.
151	
152	**Hand-wavy cap:** Two or more criteria scored **Hand-wavy** also fails the entire analysis —
153	the same bound applies: revise and re-score once, per "How to Apply This Gate" above. One
154	criterion at Hand-wavy is tolerated (one isolated weaker section does not indicate a systemic
155	quality problem); two or more at Hand-wavy indicates a pattern of shallow reasoning that the
156	gate alone cannot catch, because no single criterion has reached the gate-fail level. If two or
157	more criteria still score Hand-wavy after that single pass, the cap breach is presented as an
158	unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of being withheld.
159	
160	**Pass:** No criterion scores Absent, and at most one criterion scores Hand-wavy.
161	(Equivalently: every criterion is Sound or above, except at most one may be Hand-wavy.)
162	
163	**Escape-valve scoring (global rule, applies to every criterion):** Any section that
164	legitimately uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`) is
165	scored **Rigorous** if the stated reason is specific to this analysis — it names a property
166	of this problem that makes the section's content unnecessary — and **Hand-wavy** if the
167	reason is generic or copy-pasteable to any analysis. A properly-used escape valve is
168	**never** scored Absent solely for using the escape valve: the per-criterion Absent
169	descriptors below apply to a section that is missing, empty, or filled with non-scoreable
170	content, not to a section that is honestly and specifically marked as having no material
171	content.
172	
173	**Load-bearing chain (definition):** A derivation chain is *load-bearing* if a claim in
174	the Conclusion section (output section 6) depends on it — i.e., the chain produces, or is
175	cited as support for, a conclusion the analysis actually presents. A chain that reaches
176	only an intermediate result no conclusion rests on is not load-bearing. (This is the
177	narrower scoring sense of the phrase `SKILL.md` uses informally as "load-bearing for a
178	high-stakes conclusion.")
179	
180	---
181	
182	## Verdict Block Format
183	
184	The six verdict blocks are emitted together under the single top-level heading
185	`## Self-Audit Gate (process output)`, one `##` heading holding all six in criterion order —
186	the same placement the adversarial pass record and the self-audit scan prescribe for themselves.
187	They are one artifact, not six; nesting them beneath another section's heading makes them a
188	subsection of something they do not belong to, and a reader or a check keyed to that heading
189	must find it in the same structural position on every run.
190	
191	Each of the 6 criteria requires exactly one verdict block. Use the standard form when the
192	analysis section exists and contains scoreable content:
193	
194	```text
195	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
196	Quoted span: "[Direct quote of the specific text that most directly determines the band assigned — from the analysis being scored, or, per the admission below, from the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6 or the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2, each emitted as process output for this analysis.]"
197	Band: [**Rigorous** / **Sound** / **Hand-wavy** / **Absent**]
198	Justification: [One sentence tying the quoted span to the observable descriptor for
199	that band — name the specific structural property present or absent.]
200	```
201	
202	The self-audit scan and the Assumption Audit scan are not output sections, and they are the only artifacts outside the six-section analysis a verdict block may quote: the self-audit scan for Criteria 4 and 6, and the Assumption Audit scan for Criterion 2. Every other criterion quotes the analysis text itself, and the §6→§4 closure ledger is admitted nowhere — it is a drafting artifact that describes a document other than the one being scored.
203	
204	Use the gap-citation form when the criterion scores Absent because the section or named
205	artifact is missing or empty — in that case there is no span to quote, and the documented
206	absence is the evidence:
207	
208	```text
209	**Criterion N: [Criterion Name]**
210	Gap: [Name what is missing and where it should have appeared — e.g., "No Derivation
211	Chains section exists; chains of the form 'GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate] → [conclusion]'
212	should appear in section 4 (Derivation Chains) for each conclusion stated in section 6
213	(Conclusion)."]
214	Band: Absent
215	Justification: [One sentence: the absence itself is the structural failure that triggers
216	the gate — the criterion cannot be scored against a non-existent artifact.]
217	```
218	
219	Verdict blocks (not a consolidated table) are required because each block contains a quoted
220	span or a gap citation. Without that span, the evidence-quoting requirement cannot be audited:
221	a summary table of band labels can be produced by asserting compliance, but a verdict block
222	containing a quote that contradicts its claimed band creates a contradiction that cannot be
223	sustained.
224	
225	---
226	
227	## Criteria
228	
229	Apply all six criteria in the order listed. Criteria 1-5 follow the order of the
230	six-section output format — the same chain-of-artifacts sequence the analysis itself
231	follows — so that a scoring pass moves through the analysis in the order it was produced;
232	Criterion 6 is a whole-document cross-section check applied last.
233	
234	### Criterion 1: Identify Essence
235	
236	Scores the **Essence Statement** — the single sentence naming the core problem followed by
237	a short list of success criteria — in the Problem Essence section (output section 1).
238	
239	- **Rigorous** — the Essence Statement is a single sentence that names the core question or
240	  decision (not a symptom, not the triggering event, not a restatement of the user's prompt);
241	  each success criterion contains a pass/fail structural test — a verb + subject + outcome
242	  triplet where the outcome is a property of the Conclusion section — so that a reviewer
243	  applies each criterion by scanning the Conclusion section without analyst interpretation;
244	  the statement is specific enough that it appears nowhere in an analysis of a different but
245	  related problem without modification (it names a property unique to this problem, not a
246	  generic template phrase).
247	  If this section uses the honest-depth escape valve (`Nothing material here — [reason]`), the
248	  stated reason is specific to this analysis's problem — it names a property of the problem
249	  that makes an Essence Statement unnecessary or redundant, and that reason appears in no
250	  other analysis without alteration.
251	
252	- **Sound** — the Essence Statement exists and names a question, but the success criteria are
253	  vague or stated in terms that cannot be verified against the conclusion without further
254	  clarification (e.g., "the solution should be good," "the approach should be appropriate").
255	
256	- **Hand-wavy** — the Essence Statement exists but names a symptom, a triggering event, or a
257	  restatement of the user's prompt rather than the underlying question; OR the success criteria

Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Abandoned Reasoning section, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban, a missing `[Assumes: X]` declaration, or hop validity and arithmetic — none of which the chain-form table carries a column for — quote the analysis text directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.

385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning

174	## 4. Derivation Chains
175	
176	Show how the ground truths combine into conclusions. Every conclusion offered in this analysis must have exactly one chain here — no more (no redundant restatement), no fewer (no orphaned conclusions).
177	
178	**Chain numbering convention.** Number each `### Conclusion:` block in this section `C1`,
179	`C2`, ... in document order (e.g., `### Conclusion C1: [Conclusion text]`). The §6→§4
180	closure ledger (the agent body — `SKILL.md` on the skill surface, `agents/first-principles.md` on the agent surface — "Before presenting conclusions") cites these IDs when mapping a
181	Conclusion-section (section 6) claim back to the chain in this section that established it.
182	
183	**Chain format:**
184	
185	```text
186	GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]
187	```
188	
189	The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
190	
191	Each chain must contain at least one intermediate step. A chain that goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion is incomplete — the intermediate is where the reasoning happens. The intermediate must be a new claim that could not be stated from any single head input alone. If no intermediate can be stated, the conclusion is either a restatement of a head input (trivial) or a reasoning step is missing.
192	
193	**No-wrap rule.** A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. A chain needing more hops continues on further arrow-led lines. A hop too long for comfort is SPLIT, not wrapped — the analysis renders as Markdown, so a long hop soft-wraps for the reader without breaking the form.
194	
195	```text
196	GT-1 ([brief fact label]) + GT-6 ([brief fact label])
197	→ [intermediate claim]
198	→ [further intermediate]
199	→ [conclusion]
200	```
201	
202	**Head-input rule.** The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
203	
204	```text
205	GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])
206	→ [intermediate claim]
207	→ [conclusion]
208	```
209	
210	The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach.
211	
212	The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples.
213	
214	**Conforming — head, then one hop per line:**
215	
216	```text
217	GT-1 (Lambda $/GB-s, AWS pricing) + GT-6 (Fargate $/vCPU-hr, AWS pricing)
218	→ Lambda costs 2.10× per unit of actual compute

228	→ sustained workloads belong on Fargate

## 4. Derivation Chains

### C1 — The Carnot ceiling falsifies the 85% figure outright (theoretical-limit technique)

**Governing hard constraint:** the Second Law of Thermodynamics, expressed as the Carnot limit — no heat engine operating between two reservoirs can exceed η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, regardless of engineering quality.

```text
GT-1 (temperature conversion) + GT-2 (Carnot limit law)
→ converting 565°C and 290°C to kelvin gives T_hot = 838.15 K and two candidate T_cold readings, 563.15 K under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading or 298.15-313.15 K under an ambient-condenser reading
→ applying η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot to the literal reading yields an ideal ceiling of 32.8%
→ applying the same formula to the ambient reading yields an ideal ceiling of 62.6-64.4%
→ both ceilings sit far below the claimed 85%
→ this gap exists before any turbine, heat-exchanger, or parasitic loss is subtracted
→ an 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is therefore thermodynamically impossible for a heat engine spanning this temperature range, under either plausible reading of "290-565°C"
→ a developer who sizes a pilot against vendor marketing claiming "up to 85%" discovers the real shortfall only after financial close [Assumes: A-11]
→ that discovery shifts due-diligence practice toward demanding independently-audited efficiency guarantees for small thermal-storage projects before underwriting
→ competing Li-ion BESS vendors have a commercial incentive to publicize this exact gap [Assumes: A-12]
→ publicizing it risks suppressing capital allocation to the large-scale, long-duration thermal storage projects where the technology's real advantage actually holds
→ immediately, a 5 MWh pilot priced against an assumed 85% RTE is financially underwater from commissioning
→ real input-electricity purchase costs run several times the assumed figure, as quantified in C2 and C4
→ over decades, thermal storage's genuine long-duration cost advantage only becomes relevant at scales and durations far beyond 5 MWh
→ the technology's competitive window is therefore displaced in both scale and time from the case the claim describes, not absent outright

**Pre-check:** head GT-1, GT-2 (both unsuffixed, physical-law/definitional) · ?-marked: none · lowest cited chain: none · Inputs ceiling: HIGH
**Confidence:** HIGH — Inputs are both physical-law/definitional ground truths carrying no `?`; Inference is direct arithmetic with no intervening assumption on the core ceiling calculation (the later second-order hops carry their own flagged assumptions, A-11 and A-12 — hops 7-10 above, marked [2nd]/[3rd] actor-lens and [2nd]/[3rd] time-lens in the Assumption Audit scan — but these are consequences of the falsification, not inputs to it, and both are explicitly marked not load-bearing in the Assumptions Table); Rivals: no plausible reading of "290-565°C" raises the ceiling anywhere near 85% — even the most generous (ambient-sink) reading tops out at 64.4%, and no rival interpretation of the stated temperature pair exists that would change this.
```

### C2 — Real-architecture and small-scale derating (estimate technique, magnitude rebuild with explicit bracket)

**Target quantity:** 5 MWh-scale electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency, as a bracketed estimate.

```text
GT-3 (charge eff. ~98%) + GT-8? (utility discharge eff. ~38-40%) + GT-13? (utility storage retention ~99%, derated) + GT-9? (small-scale discharge penalty ~20-28%) + GT-11? (freeze/trace-heating parasitic)

→ that composite is a round-trip estimate of roughly 35-38% electricity-to-electricity
→ a 5 MWh system implies a power block on the order of 1 MWe [Assumes: A-05]
→ that is two orders of magnitude below the 50-100+ MWe utility-scale reference plants behind the 35-40% discharge figure in GT-8?
→ substituting the small-scale discharge penalty (~20-28%, GT-9?) [Assumes: A-06] for the utility-scale discharge figure lowers the composite
→ derating storage retention further for the small tank's higher surface-to-volume ratio and continuous freeze-protection parasitic load [Assumes: A-07] lowers the composite again
→ the resulting central estimate for a 5 MWh system's real-world round-trip efficiency is roughly 18-25% electricity-to-electricity

```

```text

→ a 5 MWh Li-ion BESS converts roughly 85-92% of charging electricity back to usable AC output (GT-7?)

→ the thermal system must therefore purchase on the order of 3.5-4.5x more input electricity to deliver the same usable output energy
→ separately, a ~1 MWe-class steam/ORC turbine-generator package carries a per-kW cost roughly 2-4x higher than equivalent utility-scale equipment [Assumes: A-09] (GT-10?)
→ that is because turbine, condenser, generator, and controls costs do not shrink proportionally with size, while the storage medium itself stays cheap per kWh at any scale
→ combining the capex disadvantage with the charging-energy multiplier means the thermal system's levelized cost per kWh of delivered electricity is higher on both the capital and the operating-energy components
→ at 5 MWh / multi-hour scale, the molten-salt thermal-electric system is therefore not cost-competitive with a same-capacity Li-ion BESS
→ the storage-medium cost advantage thermal technology holds in principle only materializes at much larger scale and longer duration than a 5 MWh system provides

**Pre-check:** head GT-7?, GT-10?, C2 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: GT-7, GT-10 · lowest cited chain: MEDIUM (C2) · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Inputs axis capped both by C2's MEDIUM band and by GT-10?'s unverified cost figures, the weakest-sourced input in this entire analysis; what would close it: a primary, itemized capex bill-of-materials for a ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block, and a current-year (not 2030-projection) NREL ATB or EIA baseline for 5 MWh-scale Li-ion installed cost. Inference: the multiplicative relationship between round-trip efficiency and charging-energy cost is a direct, uncontested consequence of the cited efficiency figures. Rivals: a rival could argue molten salt's longer tank/salt life (20-30 yr vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited 10-15 yr) offsets the capex gap over a multi-decade horizon — this rival is live and is carried forward into Section 5 rather than dismissed; it does not reverse the near-term/levelized verdict above, because it operates on a different (longevity) axis than the one the claim asserts (cost-competitiveness "of the same nameplate capacity," without a stated time horizon).
```

**Key insight:** The 85% figure is not an ambitious-but-missed engineering target — it exceeds the thermodynamic ceiling itself (62.6-64.4% under the most generous ambient-sink reading, 32.8% under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading), so no engineering improvement at any scale closes that gap for a power-to-power architecture (chain C1). The number most plausibly originates from a real but different metric: the most credible named real-world comparator, Malta Inc., reports 85-95% only as a combined heat-and-power (cogeneration) figure, not an electricity-to-electricity one — exactly the S2 conflation this analysis flagged in Section 1 (chain C3).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Molten-salt thermal storage has two genuine, non-fabricated advantages over Li-ion: a cheap storage medium per kWh, and a much longer calendar/mechanical life (20-30 years vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited 10-15 years). Neither advantage is large enough to reverse the cost-competitiveness verdict at 5 MWh / multi-hour scale, because the power-conversion equipment cost and the efficiency-driven charging-energy cost dominate at this scale; both advantages become decisive only at much larger scale and longer duration than the claim describes (chain C4).

**Sub-claim verdicts:**

| Sub-claim | Verdict | Chain |
|---|---|---|
| S1 — >85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency | False — exceeds the Carnot ceiling, not merely unlikely | C1 |
| S2 — "electricity into heat and back" means power-to-power | True as read; this is what makes S1 fail rather than merely underperform | C1, C3 |
| S3 — 5 MWh scale doesn't change the physics | False — small power-block turbomachinery and adverse surface/volume scaling plausibly cut real efficiency to ~18-25%, below even utility-scale reference figures | C2 |
| S4 — cost-competitive with same-capacity Li-ion | False, with one unresolved caveat (A-13) — power-block diseconomies of scale plus the efficiency penalty raise levelized cost on both the capital and operating-energy components, but the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is unspecified | C4 |

**What would change this conclusion:** Restricting the claim to power-to-heat delivery (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85-90% is routine and commercially demonstrated (chain C3); or restricting the power-to-power/cost comparison to utility scale (100+ MWh, long duration), where the best credible architecture (Malta's projected 55-60%) at least becomes capex-structurally relevant against large Li-ion installations — though still well under the claimed 85% (chains C1, C4). Neither restatement matches the claim as written, which specifies a 5 MWh electrical nameplate compared directly against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH) · C2 (MEDIUM) · C3 (MEDIUM) · C4 (MEDIUM) · GT-N? used directly: none (all routed through C1-C4) · lowest cited: MEDIUM (C2, C3, C4) · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM overall, but with an internal split that matters: the core physics falsification of S1 (chain C1) is **HIGH** confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim as stated — it rests only on unsuffixed, physical-law ground truths with no live rival. The magnitude estimates for S3 (chain C2, MEDIUM) and the real-world corroboration for S2/S3 (chain C3, MEDIUM) and the cost-competitiveness verdict for S4 (chain C4, MEDIUM) all carry an unverified-input discount — primarily GT-8?, GT-9?, GT-10?, and GT-11?, none of which were confirmed against a primary source in this session (three WebFetch attempts failed: a 404 on Malta's own data sheet, a 403 on the Li-ion efficiency field-data article, and a DNS failure on NREL's SolarPACES database). The Phase 5 adversarial (inversion) pass surfaced one additional, specifically cost-side caveat not previously tracked: chain C4's final hop rests on **A-13** (unverified) — that the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is a normal, representative same-duration/power-rating system — which this analysis cannot verify because the claim specifies no comparator configuration; this caveat applies only to S4 and does not touch S1's physics falsification. What would raise the overall band to HIGH: a primary, itemized capex bill-of-materials for a ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block; a primary (not WebSearch-summarized) performance report for an operating CSP plant's power-block efficiency; either a working Malta data-sheet link or an independent audit of Malta's 55-60%/85-95% figures; and a source specifying the claim's intended Li-ion comparator (A-13). None of these would overturn the headline verdict (C1 alone is already sufficient and HIGH-confidence) — they would only sharpen the magnitude of S3's and the certainty of S4's secondary conclusions.
