86	### Type Definitions and Prescribed Treatments
87	
88	**physical law** — a constraint imposed by physics, mathematics, or formal logic that cannot change regardless of context or decisions made.
89	Prescribed treatment: accept as a ground-truth candidate and record it in the Ground Truths section.
90	
91	**current constraint** — a real limitation that applies now but could change (budget, team size, regulatory environment, technology availability).
92	Prescribed treatment: record the expiry conditions — what would have to change for this constraint to no longer hold. Do not treat it as permanent.
93	
94	**convention** — a practice or standard that exists because it has been adopted, not because it is physically or logically required.
95	Prescribed treatment: explicitly challenge the convention before accepting it. "We do it this way" is not a justification.
96	
97	**untested belief** — a claim held as true that has not been empirically verified in the context of this analysis.
98	Prescribed treatment: verify it, or flag it unverified. An untested belief used in a derivation chain must be marked with the `GT-N?` notation (see Ground Truths) and any conclusion depending on it inherits a confidence caveat.
99	
100	### Stakes-Escalation Rule
101	
102	The higher the stakes of the conclusion resting on an assumption, the more that assumption must be pushed toward physical law or verified ground truth status. Classification drives the method — it does not merely label.
103	
104	### Verdict Vocabulary
105	
106	The Verdict cell is a token prefix followed by an em-dash and the justification — the bare
107	token leads so it stays matchable, and the em-dash prose carries the reasoning. **The separator
108	is an em-dash, never a colon.** `Accept: the figure is audited` puts the token and the reasoning
109	on one side of a punctuation mark that appears throughout ordinary prose, so the cell stops being
110	matchable — which is the whole property the token-first form exists to provide. Measured: a single
111	run using the colon form scored ten non-conforming verdict cells at once. The em-dash is not a
112	stylistic preference here; it is the delimiter:
113	
114	- **Accept** — the assumption survives challenge and may be used in the analysis (e.g., "Accept — survives P2 challenge; physical-law backed by GT-1")
115	- **Challenge** — the assumption is questionable; probe further before use (e.g., "Challenge — vendor benchmark unverified, flagged GT-5?")
116	- **Discard** — the assumption is false or irrelevant; remove from the reasoning chain (e.g., "Discard — contradicted by GT-2, no longer load-bearing")
117	
118	**A current-constraint verdict records its expiry at the point of use.** An assumption classified `current constraint` is accepted only until that constraint lapses; the verdict cell says when. The expiry belongs in the em-dash justification and never in the token slot — the token slot carries one of the three tokens above and nothing else.
119	
120	**Conforming — a current constraint recording its expiry:**
121	
122	```text
123	Accept — expires at term end (1 or 3 years); until then the constraint is contractual, not physical
124	```
125	
126	**Non-conforming — the expiry hoisted into the token slot:**
127	
128	```text
129	Current constraint (expires at term end) — contractual, not physical
130	```
131	
132	The vocabulary above is unchanged because run 3 rendered four current-constraint rows conformingly on the identical prompt by putting the expiry in the justification — this is a worked example, not a schema change.
133

3	# Replacement blocks
4	
5	> **Scope:** the correct-by-appending applier. Step 4 of *Deliver the analysis as a file*
6	> extracts the awk program below and runs it over `<path>.answer`, `<path>` and
7	> `<path>.process` concatenated, in that order. The agent never opens this file with Read;
8	> the contract below is the specification the program implements.
9	
10	## Contract
11	
12	The working files are append-only, so a block already appended is never rewritten in place.
13	A correction is appended as a replacement block, and step 4 swaps it in when it assembles.
14	
15	- A replacement block's first line is `## Replace: <heading text>`, where the text is the
16	  existing heading exactly as written, without its leading `#` characters. The next line is
17	  the corrected heading line, followed by its full corrected content.
18	- The target is that heading through the next heading of the same or higher level. Only `##`
19	  and `###` headings can be targets, and the replacement opens a heading of the same level.
20	- The replacement's own text runs to the next `#` or `##` heading line, which in practice is
21	  the next appended block or the next marker. A `###` replacement may therefore carry further
22	  `###` blocks after its first heading, which is how a chain is added.
23	- Replacements apply in file order. A later one for the same heading wins, including one that
24	  targets a heading an earlier replacement introduced.
25	- Several blocks may share one heredoc, so the corrections one check finds go in one call.
26	- Lines inside a fenced code block are never headings or markers.
27	- A `## Withdraw: <text>` line cancels every earlier `## Replace: <text>` block with that
28	  text. It is the only recovery for a refused replacement, because the working files are
29	  append-only.
30	- A Withdraw naming no earlier replacement does not refuse. It prints
31	  `WARNING: withdraw matched nothing: <text>` on stderr and assembly continues, so a mistyped
32	  Withdraw is harmless and is fixed by appending a correct one.
33	- Both markers are consumed. The assembled file carries no `## Replace:` or `## Withdraw:`
34	  line.
35	
36	## Refusals and recovery
37	
38	Assembly that cannot proceed prints `NOT ASSEMBLED: ...` on stderr, writes nothing, and exits
39	non-zero; `<path>.answer` and `<path>.process` stay in place.
40	
41	The four refusals a replacement block causes are: a target that matches no heading, a target
42	that matches more than one heading, a target heading of another level than the replacement,
43	and a marker not followed by a `##` or `###` heading line. Each is decided only after Withdraw
44	lines are processed, and each is cleared the same way: append `## Withdraw: <the text the
45	message quotes>`, copied from the message rather than retyped, then a corrected block if the
46	correction is still wanted, then re-issue step 4.
47	
48	A refusal for a code fence that is never closed above a marker is not cleared by a Withdraw,
49	because every line under an unclosed fence, a Withdraw included, is fenced text. Append a line
50	of exactly three backticks to close it, then a Withdraw for the replacement block whose
51	content opened the fence if one did, then re-append any correction that sat inside the fence
52	(those marker lines are now literal fenced text and are not applied). The recovery is the same
53	whether the fence was opened inside a replacement block or inside an appended section.
54	
55	## The program
56	
57	```awk
58	# Apply every "## Replace: <heading>" block, and every "## Withdraw: <text>" line, in the text read.
59	# Reads stdin or files; writes the assembled text to stdout, or prints NOT ASSEMBLED: to stderr and writes nothing.
60	# A fence line is one that starts with three backticks; a heading is a "#" line outside a fence.
61	function lvl(s,   c) {
62	  c = 0
63	  while (substr(s, c + 1, 1) == "#") c++
64	  if (c < 1 || c > 6 || substr(s, c + 1, 1) != " ") return 0
65	  return c
66	}
67	function htext(s,   t) { t = substr(s, lvl(s) + 2); sub(/[ \t\r]+$/, "", t); return t }
68	function mark(   i, f) {
69	  f = 0; fstart = 0
70	  for (i = 1; i <= m; i++) {
71	    if (substr(C[i], 1, 3) == FENCE) { f = !f; H[i] = 0; if (f) fstart = i; continue }
72	    H[i] = f ? 0 : lvl(C[i])
73	  }
74	  return f
75	}
76	function die(msg) { print "NOT ASSEMBLED: " msg > "/dev/stderr"; exit 1 }
77	BEGIN { FENCE = "\140\140\140"; PFX = "Replace: "; WPFX = "Withdraw: " }
78	{ L[++n] = $0 }
79	END {
80	  for (i = 1; i <= n; i++) C[i] = L[i]
81	  m = n
82	  if (mark()) {
83	    for (i = fstart; i <= m; i++)
84	      if (substr(C[i], 1, 3) == "## " && (substr(C[i], 4, length(PFX)) == PFX || substr(C[i], 4, length(WPFX)) == WPFX)) die("a code fence opened at line " fstart " is never closed above the marker '" substr(C[i], 4) "' - append a line of three backticks, withdraw the block that opened it if one did, re-append what sat inside it, then re-issue")
85	  }
86	  nb = 0; nr = 0; i = 1
87	  while (i <= m) {
88	    if (H[i] == 2 && substr(htext(C[i]), 1, length(WPFX)) == WPFX) {
89	      W = substr(htext(C[i]), length(WPFX) + 1)
90	      wn = 0
91	      for (r = 1; r <= nr; r++) if (T[r] == W && !X[r]) { X[r] = 1; wn++ }
92	      if (wn == 0) print "WARNING: withdraw matched nothing: " W > "/dev/stderr"
93	      i += 1
94	    } else if (H[i] == 2 && substr(htext(C[i]), 1, length(PFX)) == PFX) {
95	      T[++nr] = substr(htext(C[i]), length(PFX) + 1)
96	      j = i + 1; h = (j <= m) ? H[j] : 0
97	      BAD[nr] = (h < 2 || h > 3 || substr(htext(C[j]), 1, length(PFX)) == PFX || substr(htext(C[j]), 1, length(WPFX)) == WPFX) ? "replacement for '" T[nr] "' does not start with a ## or ### heading line" : ""
98	      k = (j <= m && h != 1) ? j + 1 : j
99	      while (k <= m && !(H[k] >= 1 && H[k] <= 2)) k++
100	      RS_[nr] = rn + 1
101	      for (q = j; q < k; q++) R[++rn] = C[q]
102	      RE_[nr] = rn; RH[nr] = h
103	      i = k
104	    } else { B[++nb] = C[i]; i++ }
105	  }
106	  for (r = 1; r <= nr; r++) if (!X[r] && BAD[r] != "") die(BAD[r])
107	  for (i = 1; i <= nb; i++) C[i] = B[i]
108	  for (i = nb + 1; i <= m; i++) delete C[i]
109	  m = nb
110	  for (r = 1; r <= nr; r++) {
111	    if (X[r]) continue
112	    mark(); cnt = 0
113	    for (i = 1; i <= m; i++) if (H[i] > 0 && htext(C[i]) == T[r]) { cnt++; at = i }
114	    if (cnt == 0) die("no heading matches '" T[r] "'")
115	    if (cnt > 1) die(cnt " headings match '" T[r] "'")
116	    if (H[at] != RH[r]) die("the replacement for '" T[r] "' opens a level-" RH[r] " heading but the target is level " H[at])
117	    e = at + 1
118	    while (e <= m && !(H[e] >= 1 && H[e] <= H[at])) e++
119	    nn = 0
120	    for (i = 1; i < at; i++) N2[++nn] = C[i]
121	    for (q = RS_[r]; q <= RE_[r]; q++) N2[++nn] = R[q]
122	    for (i = e; i <= m; i++) N2[++nn] = C[i]
123	    for (i = 1; i <= nn; i++) C[i] = N2[i]
124	    for (i = nn + 1; i <= m; i++) delete C[i]
125	    m = nn
126	  }
127	  for (i = 1; i <= m; i++) print C[i]
128	}

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Using Gemasolar's modeled solar-to-electricity figure as the power-block efficiency input

**What was tried:** Using the modeled 18.7% "solar-to-electricity" efficiency figure found for a Gemasolar-type plant (via WebSearch) as the GT-8 power-block thermal-to-electric efficiency input in chain C2.
**Why abandoned:** That figure is a whole-plant metric including optical/receiver losses upstream of the power block (heliostat field reflectivity, receiver absorption losses), not a power-block-only thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency — using it would have understated the power block's own efficiency and overstated how far the real system falls below even the utility-scale CSP figure already used.
**What it ruled out:** Conflating "solar-to-electricity" with "thermal-to-electric" as interchangeable metrics; GT-8? retains the ~38-40% engineering-estimate figure instead, flagged for its own provenance weakness rather than silently substituting a worse-fitting number that happened to be easier to find.

### Dead End: Letting molten salt's longer calendar life rescue the cost-competitiveness verdict

**What was tried:** Letting molten salt's longer tank/salt calendar life (~20-30 years, vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited ~10-15 years) reverse chain C4's cost-competitiveness verdict by amortizing the capex premium over a longer operating horizon.
**Why abandoned:** The claim's comparison basis — "cost-competitive... of the same nameplate capacity" — states no time horizon, and is most naturally read as a near-term capex/efficiency comparison. Even granting a multi-decade horizon, the thermal system's combined ~2-4x capex premium and ~3.4-5.1x round-trip efficiency penalty (chain C4) are large enough that longer calendar life alone does not close the gap without additional assumptions (Li-ion augmentation costs, discount rates) the claim does not supply and this analysis was not asked to model.
**What it ruled out:** Treating cycle life as a silent rescue of the cost claim. It remains a genuine, live advantage of thermal storage — carried forward explicitly as an unresolved rival in chain C4's confidence note and in Section 6 — rather than either dismissed or allowed to quietly flip the verdict.

### Dead End: Resolving "290-565°C" to a single authoritative Carnot-sink interpretation

**What was tried:** Resolving the ambiguity in "290-565°C" (literal two-tank-as-sink vs. ambient-condenser reading) to a single authoritative interpretation before running the Carnot calculation in chain C1.
**Why abandoned:** The claim's text does not disambiguate which reading is intended, and the verdict does not depend on resolving it: the literal reading gives a 32.8% ceiling and the ambient reading gives 62.6-64.4%, and both fall far below 85%. Picking one reading to present as "the" interpretation would have manufactured false precision about the claim's own wording rather than reflecting a genuine ambiguity.
**What it ruled out:** Any need to adjudicate the ambiguity for the headline verdict; chain C1 presents both bounding cases explicitly instead.

### Dead End: Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to Li-ion vs. molten-salt

**What was tried:** Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to formally score Li-ion vs. molten-salt storage across cost, efficiency, lifespan, and response-time criteria.
**Why abandoned:** The trade-off procedure is designed for selecting among viable options in a live decision ("which should I choose"). This analysis verifies a comparative truth claim ("is X cost-competitive with Y"), not a decision with options surviving a must-have knockout filter — there is no "choice" to weight and score here; a formal weighted scorecard would restate chains C2-C4's conclusions in a different format without adding evidence.

```text
**What would change this conclusion:** Restricting the claim to power-to-heat delivery (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85-90% is routine and commercially demonstrated (chain C3); or restricting the power-to-power/cost comparison to utility scale (100+ MWh, long duration), where the best credible architecture (Malta's projected 55-60%) at least becomes capex-structurally relevant against large Li-ion installations — though still well under the claimed 85% (chains C1, C4). Neither restatement matches the claim as written, which specifies a 5 MWh electrical nameplate compared directly against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH) · C2 (MEDIUM) · C3 (MEDIUM) · C4 (MEDIUM) · GT-N? used directly: none (all routed through C1-C4) · lowest cited: MEDIUM (C2, C3, C4) · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM overall, but with an internal split that matters: the core physics falsification of S1 (chain C1) is **HIGH** confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim as stated — it rests only on unsuffixed, physical-law ground truths with no live rival. The magnitude estimates for S3 (chain C2, MEDIUM) and the real-world corroboration for S2/S3 (chain C3, MEDIUM) and the cost-competitiveness verdict for S4 (chain C4, MEDIUM) all carry an unverified-input discount — primarily GT-8?, GT-9?, GT-10?, and GT-11?, none of which were confirmed against a primary source in this session (three WebFetch attempts failed: a 404 on Malta's own data sheet, a 403 on the Li-ion efficiency field-data article, and a DNS failure on NREL's SolarPACES database). The Phase 5 adversarial (inversion) pass surfaced one additional, specifically cost-side caveat not previously tracked: chain C4's final hop rests on **A-13** (unverified) — that the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is a normal, representative same-duration/power-rating system — which this analysis cannot verify because the claim specifies no comparator configuration; this caveat applies only to S4 and does not touch S1's physics falsification. What would raise the overall band to HIGH: a primary, itemized capex bill-of-materials for a ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block; a primary (not WebSearch-summarized) performance report for an operating CSP plant's power-block efficiency; either a working Malta data-sheet link or an independent audit of Malta's 55-60%/85-95% figures; and a source specifying the claim's intended Li-ion comparator (A-13). None of these would overturn the headline verdict (C1 alone is already sufficient and HIGH-confidence) — they would only sharpen the magnitude of S3's and the certainty of S4's secondary conclusions.
```

Analyze the following claim from first principles. Decompose it into its constituent sub-claims, establish ground-truth physical and economic facts, challenge every assumption, and reason upward to a validated conclusion (accept, reject, or qualify).

CLAIM: "A 5 MWh molten-salt thermal energy storage tank operating at 290-565 °C can round-trip electricity into heat and back with a system efficiency above 85%, making it cost-competitive with a lithium-ion battery system of the same nameplate capacity."

Things to decompose and check explicitly:

1. The physics of the round trip. Electricity-to-heat (resistive heating or heat pump) is typically near 100% efficient at the heating step itself, but the claim is about "electricity into heat and BACK" — i.e., heat-to-electricity reconversion, which runs through a thermodynamic heat engine (e.g., Rankine cycle, ORC, sCO2 cycle, or Brayton/Carnot-limited device) bounded by the Carnot limit between the hot salt temperature (~565°C / 838K) and the cold/ambient sink (~290°C floor on the "cold" tank, or true ambient ~300K if it's a full discharge path). Compute the Carnot ceiling for realistic hot/cold reservoir pairs and compare to 85%.
2. Whether "290-565°C" describes the hot/cold tank pair of a two-tank molten salt system (i.e., the cold tank is NOT ambient — it's 290°C) and what that implies for how much exergy is actually recoverable, versus if the claim conflates round-trip "efficiency" of just the charge/storage/heat delivery (thermal output) with round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency (this is the classic distinction between "power-to-heat" storage with near-unity efficiency and "power-to-power" / Carnot-battery systems with real-world round-trip efficiencies typically 40-60%, rarely above 70%, under current commercial technology).
3. Real-world reference points: known thermal/Carnot battery projects (e.g., Siemens Gamesa ETES, Malta Inc., Highview Power LAES, Azelio, SaltX, Fortum/commercial CSP-derived systems) and what round-trip efficiencies they actually claim/achieve.
4. Scale effects: is 5 MWh (a small, likely behind-the-meter or pilot scale) consistent with claimed efficiency, given that smaller systems suffer proportionally larger heat losses, lower turbine/heat-exchanger efficiency, and worse parasitic loads than utility-scale (100+ MWh) systems?
5. The cost-competitiveness sub-claim: compare $/kWh capex and $/kWh-cycle levelized cost for a 5 MWh thermal-electric storage system (accounting for its needed power conversion equipment: heaters, heat exchangers, turbine/generator or ORC unit) against a 5 MWh lithium-ion BESS, which at this small scale has a very different cost structure (power electronics and BOS dominate at small scale, cells are commodity-priced) — and the fact that li-ion round-trip efficiency is empirically 90-95%, so efficiency alone already seems to disfavor the claim.
6. Second-order considerations: cycle life and degradation, response time/power density (thermal systems have poor ramp rates and power-to-energy ratios vs Li-ion), siting/footprint, insulation losses over time if not cycled, and whether a "5 MWh" thermal system can even deliver the implied power rating affordably.

Produce a verdict on the overall claim (true, false, or needs qualification) and explain precisely which sub-claims are physically plausible and which are not, citing the Carnot-limit math and real-world round-trip efficiency figures. Keep the final output well-organized but not padded — this will be relayed directly to an engineering-literate user who wants rigor, not a general audience explainer.

1	# Molten-Salt Thermal Storage Round-Trip Efficiency Claim
2	
3	*First-principles analysis · 15 October 2026*
4	
5	*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261015T032239Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*
6	
7	## Executive Summary
8	
9	**Recommendation:** Reject the claim. An 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically unreachable for a heat engine spanning 290-565°C under any plausible reading of that range — the Carnot ceiling itself is only 62.6-64.4% (ambient-sink reading) or 32.8% (literal two-tank-as-sink reading) (chain C1). The cost-competitiveness comparison to a same-capacity Li-ion BESS fails independently, driven by small-scale power-block diseconomies and the efficiency shortfall (chain C4).
10	
11	**Band (from §6):** MEDIUM overall — the core physics falsification (chain C1) is HIGH confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim; the magnitude and cost conclusions (chains C2, C3, C4) are MEDIUM, each capped by unverified inputs.
12	
13	**Would change it:** A primary, audited source showing a deployed molten-salt/Carnot-battery architecture at or above 62.6% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency would narrow chain C2's gap (though not validate "85%"); a primary itemized capex comparison showing the thermal system installed at or below a same-duration Li-ion BESS's cost would overturn chain C4; neither would overturn chain C1, which rests only on unsuffixed physical-law ground truths (GT-1, GT-2).
14	
15	## 1. Problem Essence
16	
17	**Essence Statement:** Does a 5 MWh molten-salt thermal energy storage (TES) system cycling between 290°C and 565°C deliver electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency above 85%, and if so (or even if not), is it cost-competitive with a 5 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) of the same nameplate capacity?
18	
19	**Success criteria a correct answer must achieve:**
20	- Resolves whether 85% round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency is physically achievable at the stated temperatures, using an explicit Carnot-limit calculation, not an appeal to vendor marketing.
21	- Distinguishes "round-trip efficiency" as power-to-power from power-to-heat (cogeneration) framings, since these are different physical quantities often conflated in industry literature.
22	- Addresses whether 5 MWh scale changes the physically/economically achievable efficiency and cost relative to the utility-scale reference systems that most published figures describe.
23	- Produces a cost-competitiveness verdict against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS grounded in capex structure (power-block diseconomies of scale vs. BESS power-electronics/BOS structure) and in the efficiency figure established above — not treated as a separate, unlinked question.
24	- Does not require the answer to be "accept" or "reject" as a forced binary — a qualified verdict (true only under a restated claim) is an admissible and, if warranted, correct output.
25	
26	**Note on framing:** The question as posed already supplies substantial technical scaffolding (the Carnot-limit framing, named reference projects, the power-to-heat vs. power-to-power distinction). This essence statement treats that scaffolding as the user's own correct intuition to be verified, not as a given to be assumed true — each element is independently checked in Phases 2-4 below.
27	
28	## 2. Assumptions Table
29	
30	![Assumption verdict matrix: assumption types against verdicts](report-20261015T032239Z-fig-verdicts.svg)
31	
32	| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
33	|---|---|---|---|---|
34	| A-01: A heat-to-electricity conversion step is bounded above by the Carnot limit η ≤ 1 − T_cold/T_hot (K) | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate | **Accept** — confirmed as the applicable bound; physical law, not subject to engineering mitigation | Second Law of Thermodynamics; not domain-specific, applies to any heat engine (Rankine, ORC, Brayton, sCO₂) regardless of working fluid or engineering quality |
35	| A-02: Resistive (Joule) electricity-to-heat conversion is ~97-99% efficient | physical law / direct measurement | Accept | **Accept** — confirmed; standard electrical-engineering result, not contested by the claim itself | Standard electrical engineering result; not contested by any source found and not the locus of dispute in this claim |
36	| A-03: "Round-trip" in the claim means electricity-to-electricity, not electricity-to-delivered-heat | convention (terminology) | Challenge explicitly — industry usage is inconsistent | **Challenge** — industry usage of "round-trip efficiency" is inconsistent, but the claim's own wording resolves to the power-to-power reading | The claim's own text ("electricity into heat and **back**") and its comparison basis ("nameplate capacity" of a BESS, an electrical rating) both specify electrical output; resolved by textual analysis, not by assumption |
37	| A-04: Vendor-reported power-to-power RTE figures (Malta 55-60%, Siemens Gamesa ~45-50%) are accurate | untested belief | Flag as unverified — self-reported by commercial entities with a commercial interest in favorable figures; Malta's own material states these are *projected* full-scale figures, not yet validated end-to-end | **Challenge** — self-reported by commercial entities with a commercial interest in favorable figures, flagged GT-4?/GT-5? | No independent third-party audit of either figure located in this analysis; treated as directional evidence only, not as proof |
38	| A-05: 5 MWh capacity implies a power block on the order of ~1 MWe (i.e., a multi-hour discharge duration) | untested belief | The claim does not state a power rating or duration; this is inferred from typical BESS/TES project conventions (2-5h duration is standard for both technologies at this capacity) | **Challenge** — no power rating is stated in the claim; inferred from typical BESS/TES duration conventions, conservative in the claim's favor | Flagged; if duration were much shorter (higher MWe) the scale penalty in chain C2 would be *more* severe, not less |
39	| A-06: Small-scale (~1 MWe) steam/ORC turbine-generator efficiency is materially worse than utility-scale (50-100+ MWe) equivalents | current constraint | Record expiry condition: this is a *current* manufacturing/engineering-economics constraint; could narrow with advances in small-scale ORC or microturbine design | **Accept** — expires if small-turbine-efficiency R&D closes the gap; current constraint, flagged for provenance (no case study located) | Engineering-judgment estimate (20-28% thermal-to-electric at ~1 MWe vs. ~38-40% at CSP utility scale), not sourced to a specific case study — flagged `?` |
40	| A-07: Solar nitrate salt requires continuous trace heating below ~220°C to prevent freezing, imposing a standing parasitic load | current constraint | Record expiry condition: specific to nitrate salt chemistry; chloride or other salt blends under active R&D have different freeze points | **Accept** — expires if an alternative low-freeze salt chemistry displaces solar salt; current constraint, corroborated by two secondary academic sources | Materials-science fact, corroborated by two independent secondary academic sources; not independently re-verified by a fresh primary-source read in this session, so flagged `?` for provenance |
41	| A-08: Li-ion AC-AC round-trip efficiency for 2024-2025 utility/commercial-scale systems is 85-92%, best-in-class >88% | untested belief → tested | Verify via source | **Challenge** — secondary field-monitoring aggregation, not a primary dataset; a direct WebFetch of the article returned HTTP 403 | batteryindustry.net / Accure field-monitoring summary — flagged `?` for provenance strength |
42	| A-09: 5 MWh Li-ion BESS all-in installed cost is $270-450/kWh and 5 MWh thermal-electric system cost is $500-900+/kWh at this scale | untested belief | Flag as engineering estimate; the NREL ATB search did not yield a precise current-year ($/kWh) baseline | **Challenge** — NREL ATB search returned only 2030/2050 projections, not a confirmed present-day baseline; the single most consequential unverified input in this analysis | No primary cost source opened; load-bearing input to the cost-competitiveness conclusion (chain C4) |
43	| A-10: The ambient/condenser sink temperature for a Rankine/ORC discharge cycle is in the 25-40°C range | convention | Minor — affects the Carnot ceiling by only ~2 percentage points across this range; does not change any conclusion | **Accept** — standard power-plant condenser design range; immaterial to the verdict either way (±2 points on the Carnot ceiling) | Standard power-plant condenser design range; not a load-bearing assumption |
44	| A-11: A developer sizing a pilot against vendor-marketed "up to 85%"-style figures would discover the real shortfall only after financial close, shifting due-diligence practice toward demanding independently-audited efficiency guarantees | untested belief | Flag as unverified — a speculative behavioral/market-response claim, not a measured fact; surfaced by the end-of-phase Assumption Audit (chain C1's second-order actor-lens extension) | **Challenge** — speculative behavioral/market-response claim with no case study located; not load-bearing for the headline verdict | No case study of an actual project discovering this shortfall post-financing was located; supports only the second-order narrative on chain C1 |
45	| A-12: Competing Li-ion BESS vendors would use the efficiency gap identified in this analysis as a competitive marketing point against thermal-storage entrants | untested belief | Flag as unverified — a speculative market-behavior claim; surfaced by the end-of-phase Assumption Audit (chain C1's second-order actor-lens extension) | **Challenge** — speculative market-behavior claim with no evidence sought or found; not load-bearing for the headline verdict | No evidence of this specific competitive dynamic was sought or found; included only as a plausible second-order consequence |
46	| A-13: The Li-ion BESS comparator implied by the claim's "same nameplate capacity" phrasing is a normal, representative same-duration/power-rating system, not an atypical or unusually expensive configuration | untested belief | Flag as unverified — surfaced by the Phase 5 adversarial (inversion) pass as a load-bearing precondition of the cost-competitiveness conclusion specifically | **Challenge** — the claim specifies no Li-ion comparator configuration to verify against; load-bearing for S4/chain C4 only, not for S1/chain C1 | No source specifies the claim's intended Li-ion comparator; carried as an explicit confidence caveat on chain C4 and in Section 6 |
47	
48	**End-of-phase note:** A-04 and A-09 are the two assumptions carrying the most weight on the final verdict's confidence (efficiency claim and cost claim respectively). Both are flagged `?` and are **not** load-bearing in the sense of being able to flip the headline verdict — A-04's upper bound (60%) and A-09's directional cost disadvantage both still fail the claim even in the most favorable plausible reading — but they do set the confidence band on the *magnitude* statements (chains C2-C4) at MEDIUM rather than HIGH. A-11 and A-12, added by the end-of-phase Assumption Audit, support only the speculative second-order narrative on chain C1 and are explicitly flagged as not load-bearing for the headline physics falsification, which rests solely on A-01/A-02 (GT-1, GT-2). A-13, added by the Phase 5 adversarial (inversion) pass, is the one unresolved load-bearing precondition behind the cost-competitiveness conclusion (S4) specifically — it does not touch S1's physics falsification, which remains unconditioned on any cost-side assumption.

74	### C1 — The Carnot ceiling falsifies the 85% figure outright (theoretical-limit technique)
75	
76	**Governing hard constraint:** the Second Law of Thermodynamics, expressed as the Carnot limit — no heat engine operating between two reservoirs can exceed η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, regardless of engineering quality.
77	
78	```text
79	GT-1 (temperature conversion) + GT-2 (Carnot limit law)
80	→ converting 565°C and 290°C to kelvin gives T_hot = 838.15 K and two candidate T_cold readings, 563.15 K under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading or 298.15-313.15 K under an ambient-condenser reading
81	→ applying η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot to the literal reading yields an ideal ceiling of 32.8%

83	→ both ceilings sit far below the claimed 85%
84	→ this gap exists before any turbine, heat-exchanger, or parasitic loss is subtracted
85	→ an 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is therefore thermodynamically impossible for a heat engine spanning this temperature range, under either plausible reading of "290-565°C"

99	### C2 — Real-architecture and small-scale derating (estimate technique, magnitude rebuild with explicit bracket)

101	**Target quantity:** 5 MWh-scale electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency, as a bracketed estimate.
102	
103	```text
104	GT-3 (charge eff. ~98%) + GT-8? (utility discharge eff. ~38-40%) + GT-13? (utility storage retention ~99%, derated) + GT-9? (small-scale discharge penalty ~20-28%) + GT-11? (freeze/trace-heating parasitic)
105	→ multiplying charge efficiency (~98%, GT-3) by utility-scale storage retention (~95-97%, derated from GT-13?'s 99% figure for real trace-heating parasitics) by utility-scale discharge efficiency (~38-40%, GT-8?) gives the utility-scale composite
106	→ that composite is a round-trip estimate of roughly 35-38% electricity-to-electricity
107	→ a 5 MWh system implies a power block on the order of 1 MWe [Assumes: A-05]
108	→ that is two orders of magnitude below the 50-100+ MWe utility-scale reference plants behind the 35-40% discharge figure in GT-8?
109	→ substituting the small-scale discharge penalty (~20-28%, GT-9?) [Assumes: A-06] for the utility-scale discharge figure lowers the composite
110	→ derating storage retention further for the small tank's higher surface-to-volume ratio and continuous freeze-protection parasitic load [Assumes: A-07] lowers the composite again
111	→ the resulting central estimate for a 5 MWh system's real-world round-trip efficiency is roughly 18-25% electricity-to-electricity
112	→ both bracket ends (18% and 25%) drive the same conclusion relative to the claimed 85% and to the utility-scale figures in C3, so the decision-resolution stop criterion is satisfied without tightening the bracket further
113	
114	**Pre-check:** head GT-3, GT-8?, GT-9?, GT-11?, GT-13? · ?-marked: GT-8, GT-9, GT-11, GT-13 · lowest cited chain: none · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
115	**Confidence:** MEDIUM — Inputs axis is short: four of five head inputs are unverified or reported-by-delegate estimates; what would close it: a primary technical case study or vendor datasheet for an actual ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block (cost and efficiency), and a primary (not WebSearch-summarized) CSP plant performance report. Inference: each hop follows directly given the stated inputs. Rivals: a rival could cite Malta's higher 55-60% power-to-power figure (C3) for utility-scale systems, but that figure (a) applies to a fundamentally more complex heat-pump-based architecture, not the simple resistive-heater charging the claim implies, and (b) is itself a projected, not yet end-to-end-validated figure (C3) — addressed on C3, and even at 55-60% utility-scale the 85% claim still fails, so this rival does not change the verdict.
116	```

120	```text

122	→ the best publicly claimed power-to-power round-trip efficiency among named molten-salt-class storage developers is Malta's projected 55-60%
123	→ that figure is not yet validated end-to-end at full scale, per the sources located in this analysis
124	→ Malta's separate 85-95% figure is explicitly a cogeneration number, crediting delivered process heat alongside electricity
125	→ a cogeneration figure is a categorically different quantity from electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency, and is the most plausible real-world origin of an "85%" headline claim
126	→ Siemens Gamesa's simpler resistive-heater architecture, structurally closer to the claim's wording, is reported at only 45-50%

139	→ a 5 MWh Li-ion BESS converts roughly 85-92% of charging electricity back to usable AC output (GT-7?)

150	```
151	
152	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
153	
154	### Dead End: Using Gemasolar's modeled solar-to-electricity figure as the power-block efficiency input
155	
156	**What was tried:** Using the modeled 18.7% "solar-to-electricity" efficiency figure found for a Gemasolar-type plant (via WebSearch) as the GT-8 power-block thermal-to-electric efficiency input in chain C2.
157	
158	**Why abandoned:** That figure is a whole-plant metric including optical/receiver losses upstream of the power block (heliostat field reflectivity, receiver absorption losses), not a power-block-only thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency — using it would have understated the power block's own efficiency and overstated how far the real system falls below even the utility-scale CSP figure already used.
159	
160	**What it ruled out:** Conflating "solar-to-electricity" with "thermal-to-electric" as interchangeable metrics; GT-8? retains the ~38-40% engineering-estimate figure instead, flagged for its own provenance weakness rather than silently substituting a worse-fitting number that happened to be easier to find.
161	
162	### Dead End: Letting molten salt's longer calendar life rescue the cost-competitiveness verdict
163	
164	**What was tried:** Letting molten salt's longer tank/salt calendar life (~20-30 years, vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited ~10-15 years) reverse chain C4's cost-competitiveness verdict by amortizing the capex premium over a longer operating horizon.
165	
166	**Why abandoned:** The claim's comparison basis — "cost-competitive... of the same nameplate capacity" — states no time horizon, and is most naturally read as a near-term capex/efficiency comparison. Even granting a multi-decade horizon, the thermal system's combined ~2-4x capex premium and ~3.4-5.1x round-trip efficiency penalty (chain C4) are large enough that longer calendar life alone does not close the gap without additional assumptions (Li-ion augmentation costs, discount rates) the claim does not supply and this analysis was not asked to model.
167	
168	**What it ruled out:** Treating cycle life as a silent rescue of the cost claim. It remains a genuine, live advantage of thermal storage — carried forward explicitly as an unresolved rival in chain C4's confidence note and in Section 6 — rather than either dismissed or allowed to quietly flip the verdict.
169	
170	### Dead End: Resolving "290-565°C" to a single authoritative Carnot-sink interpretation
171	
172	**What was tried:** Resolving the ambiguity in "290-565°C" (literal two-tank-as-sink vs. ambient-condenser reading) to a single authoritative interpretation before running the Carnot calculation in chain C1.
173	
174	**Why abandoned:** The claim's text does not disambiguate which reading is intended, and the verdict does not depend on resolving it: the literal reading gives a 32.8% ceiling and the ambient reading gives 62.6-64.4%, and both fall far below 85%. Picking one reading to present as "the" interpretation would have manufactured false precision about the claim's own wording rather than reflecting a genuine ambiguity.
175	
176	**What it ruled out:** Any need to adjudicate the ambiguity for the headline verdict; chain C1 presents both bounding cases explicitly instead.
177	
178	### Dead End: Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to Li-ion vs. molten-salt
179	
180	**What was tried:** Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to formally score Li-ion vs. molten-salt storage across cost, efficiency, lifespan, and response-time criteria.
181	
182	**Why abandoned:** The trade-off procedure is designed for selecting among viable options in a live decision ("which should I choose"). This analysis verifies a comparative truth claim ("is X cost-competitive with Y"), not a decision with options surviving a must-have knockout filter — there is no "choice" to weight and score here; a formal weighted scorecard would restate chains C2-C4's conclusions in a different format without adding evidence.
183	
184	**What it ruled out:** Treating this as a selection decision; it is a claim-verification task, so the trade-off procedure's trigger condition (two or more viable options surviving as a live choice) does not fire, and the procedure is recorded as not applicable in the Techniques not applied block (Appendix).
185	
186	### Dead End: Applying the fishbone procedure to the assumption space
187	
188	**What was tried:** Using the fishbone (breadth-first, categorical) brainstorming technique to enumerate the assumption space in Phase 2.
189	
190	**Why abandoned:** The assumption space here is a bounded, well-structured physics-plus-economics decomposition with a small number of clearly identifiable load-bearing variables (temperatures, efficiency figures, cost figures) — not a multi-causal diagnostic problem ("why does X keep happening") where intuition cannot enumerate the cause space confidently. Direct enumeration in the Assumptions Table (Section 2) was tractable without a categorical brainstorm.
191	
192	**What it ruled out:** A fishbone pass would not have surfaced assumptions beyond those already in Section 2; recorded as not applicable in the Techniques not applied block (Appendix).
193	
194	## 6. Conclusion
195	
196	**Recommended approach:** Reject the claim as stated. An 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically unreachable for a heat engine spanning 290-565°C under any plausible reading of that temperature pair, and the cost-competitiveness comparison to a same-capacity Li-ion BESS fails independently, driven by small-scale power-block diseconomies and the efficiency shortfall itself (chain C1, chain C4).
197	
198	**Key insight:** The 85% figure is not an ambitious-but-missed engineering target — it exceeds the thermodynamic ceiling itself (62.6-64.4% under the most generous ambient-sink reading, 32.8% under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading), so no engineering improvement at any scale closes that gap for a power-to-power architecture (chain C1). The number most plausibly originates from a real but different metric: the most credible named real-world comparator, Malta Inc., reports 85-95% only as a combined heat-and-power (cogeneration) figure, not an electricity-to-electricity one — exactly the S2 conflation this analysis flagged in Section 1 (chain C3).
199	
200	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Molten-salt thermal storage has two genuine, non-fabricated advantages over Li-ion: a cheap storage medium per kWh, and a much longer calendar/mechanical life (20-30 years vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited 10-15 years). Neither advantage is large enough to reverse the cost-competitiveness verdict at 5 MWh / multi-hour scale, because the power-conversion equipment cost and the efficiency-driven charging-energy cost dominate at this scale; both advantages become decisive only at much larger scale and longer duration than the claim describes (chain C4).
201	
202	**Sub-claim verdicts:**
203	
204	| Sub-claim | Verdict | Chain |
205	|---|---|---|
206	| S1 — >85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency | False — exceeds the Carnot ceiling, not merely unlikely | C1 |
207	| S2 — "electricity into heat and back" means power-to-power | True as read; this is what makes S1 fail rather than merely underperform | C1, C3 |
208	| S3 — 5 MWh scale doesn't change the physics | False — small power-block turbomachinery and adverse surface/volume scaling plausibly cut real efficiency to ~18-25%, below even utility-scale reference figures | C2 |
209	| S4 — cost-competitive with same-capacity Li-ion | False, with one unresolved caveat (A-13) — power-block diseconomies of scale plus the efficiency penalty raise levelized cost on both the capital and operating-energy components, but the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is unspecified | C4 |
210	
211	**What would change this conclusion:** Restricting the claim to power-to-heat delivery (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85-90% is routine and commercially demonstrated (chain C3); or restricting the power-to-power/cost comparison to utility scale (100+ MWh, long duration), where the best credible architecture (Malta's projected 55-60%) at least becomes capex-structurally relevant against large Li-ion installations — though still well under the claimed 85% (chains C1, C4). Neither restatement matches the claim as written, which specifies a 5 MWh electrical nameplate compared directly against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.
212	
213	**Confidence:** MEDIUM overall, but with an internal split that matters: the core physics falsification of S1 (chain C1) is **HIGH** confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim as stated — it rests only on unsuffixed, physical-law ground truths with no live rival. The magnitude estimates for S3 (chain C2, MEDIUM) and the real-world corroboration for S2/S3 (chain C3, MEDIUM) and the cost-competitiveness verdict for S4 (chain C4, MEDIUM) all carry an unverified-input discount — primarily GT-8?, GT-9?, GT-10?, and GT-11?, none of which were confirmed against a primary source in this session (three WebFetch attempts failed: a 404 on Malta's own data sheet, a 403 on the Li-ion efficiency field-data article, and a DNS failure on NREL's SolarPACES database). The Phase 5 adversarial (inversion) pass surfaced one additional, specifically cost-side caveat not previously tracked: chain C4's final hop rests on **A-13** (unverified) — that the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is a normal, representative same-duration/power-rating system — which this analysis cannot verify because the claim specifies no comparator configuration; this caveat applies only to S4 and does not touch S1's physics falsification. What would raise the overall band to HIGH: a primary, itemized capex bill-of-materials for a ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block; a primary (not WebSearch-summarized) performance report for an operating CSP plant's power-block efficiency; either a working Malta data-sheet link or an independent audit of Malta's 55-60%/85-95% figures; and a source specifying the claim's intended Li-ion comparator (A-13). None of these would overturn the headline verdict (C1 alone is already sufficient and HIGH-confidence) — they would only sharpen the magnitude of S3's and the certainty of S4's secondary conclusions.

# Molten-Salt Thermal Storage Round-Trip Efficiency Claim

*First-principles analysis · 15 October 2026*

*Read with: [How to read this analysis](HOW-TO-READ.md) · [Working file](analysis-20261015T032239Z.md) · [All files](INDEX.md)*

## Executive Summary

**Recommendation:** Reject the claim. An 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically unreachable for a heat engine spanning 290-565°C under any plausible reading of that range — the Carnot ceiling itself is only 62.6-64.4% (ambient-sink reading) or 32.8% (literal two-tank-as-sink reading) (chain C1). The cost-competitiveness comparison to a same-capacity Li-ion BESS fails independently, driven by small-scale power-block diseconomies and the efficiency shortfall (chain C4).

**Band (from §6):** MEDIUM overall — the core physics falsification (chain C1) is HIGH confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim; the magnitude and cost conclusions (chains C2, C3, C4) are MEDIUM, each capped by unverified inputs.

**Would change it:** A primary, audited source showing a deployed molten-salt/Carnot-battery architecture at or above 62.6% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency would narrow chain C2's gap (though not validate "85%"); a primary itemized capex comparison showing the thermal system installed at or below a same-duration Li-ion BESS's cost would overturn chain C4; neither would overturn chain C1, which rests only on unsuffixed physical-law ground truths (GT-1, GT-2).

## 1. Problem Essence

**Essence Statement:** Does a 5 MWh molten-salt thermal energy storage (TES) system cycling between 290°C and 565°C deliver electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency above 85%, and if so (or even if not), is it cost-competitive with a 5 MWh lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) of the same nameplate capacity?

**Success criteria a correct answer must achieve:**
- Resolves whether 85% round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency is physically achievable at the stated temperatures, using an explicit Carnot-limit calculation, not an appeal to vendor marketing.
- Distinguishes "round-trip efficiency" as power-to-power from power-to-heat (cogeneration) framings, since these are different physical quantities often conflated in industry literature.
- Addresses whether 5 MWh scale changes the physically/economically achievable efficiency and cost relative to the utility-scale reference systems that most published figures describe.
- Produces a cost-competitiveness verdict against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS grounded in capex structure (power-block diseconomies of scale vs. BESS power-electronics/BOS structure) and in the efficiency figure established above — not treated as a separate, unlinked question.
- Does not require the answer to be "accept" or "reject" as a forced binary — a qualified verdict (true only under a restated claim) is an admissible and, if warranted, correct output.

**Note on framing:** The question as posed already supplies substantial technical scaffolding (the Carnot-limit framing, named reference projects, the power-to-heat vs. power-to-power distinction). This essence statement treats that scaffolding as the user's own correct intuition to be verified, not as a given to be assumed true — each element is independently checked in Phases 2-4 below.

### C1 — The Carnot ceiling falsifies the 85% figure outright (theoretical-limit technique)

**Governing hard constraint:** the Second Law of Thermodynamics, expressed as the Carnot limit — no heat engine operating between two reservoirs can exceed η = 1 − T_cold/T_hot, regardless of engineering quality.

```text
GT-1 (temperature conversion) + GT-2 (Carnot limit law)
→ converting 565°C and 290°C to kelvin gives T_hot = 838.15 K and two candidate T_cold readings, 563.15 K under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading or 298.15-313.15 K under an ambient-condenser reading
→ applying η_Carnot = 1 − T_cold/T_hot to the literal reading yields an ideal ceiling of 32.8%
→ applying the same formula to the ambient reading yields an ideal ceiling of 62.6-64.4%
→ both ceilings sit far below the claimed 85%
→ this gap exists before any turbine, heat-exchanger, or parasitic loss is subtracted
→ an 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is therefore thermodynamically impossible for a heat engine spanning this temperature range, under either plausible reading of "290-565°C"
→ a developer who sizes a pilot against vendor marketing claiming "up to 85%" discovers the real shortfall only after financial close [Assumes: A-11]
→ that discovery shifts due-diligence practice toward demanding independently-audited efficiency guarantees for small thermal-storage projects before underwriting
→ competing Li-ion BESS vendors have a commercial incentive to publicize this exact gap [Assumes: A-12]
→ publicizing it risks suppressing capital allocation to the large-scale, long-duration thermal storage projects where the technology's real advantage actually holds
→ immediately, a 5 MWh pilot priced against an assumed 85% RTE is financially underwater from commissioning
→ real input-electricity purchase costs run several times the assumed figure, as quantified in C2 and C4
→ over decades, thermal storage's genuine long-duration cost advantage only becomes relevant at scales and durations far beyond 5 MWh
→ the technology's competitive window is therefore displaced in both scale and time from the case the claim describes, not absent outright
```

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Using Gemasolar's modeled solar-to-electricity figure as the power-block efficiency input

**What was tried:** Using the modeled 18.7% "solar-to-electricity" efficiency figure found for a Gemasolar-type plant (via WebSearch) as the GT-8 power-block thermal-to-electric efficiency input in chain C2.

**Why abandoned:** That figure is a whole-plant metric including optical/receiver losses upstream of the power block (heliostat field reflectivity, receiver absorption losses), not a power-block-only thermal-to-electric conversion efficiency — using it would have understated the power block's own efficiency and overstated how far the real system falls below even the utility-scale CSP figure already used.

**What it ruled out:** Conflating "solar-to-electricity" with "thermal-to-electric" as interchangeable metrics; GT-8? retains the ~38-40% engineering-estimate figure instead, flagged for its own provenance weakness rather than silently substituting a worse-fitting number that happened to be easier to find.

### Dead End: Letting molten salt's longer calendar life rescue the cost-competitiveness verdict

**What was tried:** Letting molten salt's longer tank/salt calendar life (~20-30 years, vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited ~10-15 years) reverse chain C4's cost-competitiveness verdict by amortizing the capex premium over a longer operating horizon.

**Why abandoned:** The claim's comparison basis — "cost-competitive... of the same nameplate capacity" — states no time horizon, and is most naturally read as a near-term capex/efficiency comparison. Even granting a multi-decade horizon, the thermal system's combined ~2-4x capex premium and ~3.4-5.1x round-trip efficiency penalty (chain C4) are large enough that longer calendar life alone does not close the gap without additional assumptions (Li-ion augmentation costs, discount rates) the claim does not supply and this analysis was not asked to model.

**What it ruled out:** Treating cycle life as a silent rescue of the cost claim. It remains a genuine, live advantage of thermal storage — carried forward explicitly as an unresolved rival in chain C4's confidence note and in Section 6 — rather than either dismissed or allowed to quietly flip the verdict.

### Dead End: Resolving "290-565°C" to a single authoritative Carnot-sink interpretation

**What was tried:** Resolving the ambiguity in "290-565°C" (literal two-tank-as-sink vs. ambient-condenser reading) to a single authoritative interpretation before running the Carnot calculation in chain C1.

**Why abandoned:** The claim's text does not disambiguate which reading is intended, and the verdict does not depend on resolving it: the literal reading gives a 32.8% ceiling and the ambient reading gives 62.6-64.4%, and both fall far below 85%. Picking one reading to present as "the" interpretation would have manufactured false precision about the claim's own wording rather than reflecting a genuine ambiguity.

**What it ruled out:** Any need to adjudicate the ambiguity for the headline verdict; chain C1 presents both bounding cases explicitly instead.

### Dead End: Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to Li-ion vs. molten-salt

**What was tried:** Applying the trade-off (weighted-criteria) procedure to formally score Li-ion vs. molten-salt storage across cost, efficiency, lifespan, and response-time criteria.

**Why abandoned:** The trade-off procedure is designed for selecting among viable options in a live decision ("which should I choose"). This analysis verifies a comparative truth claim ("is X cost-competitive with Y"), not a decision with options surviving a must-have knockout filter — there is no "choice" to weight and score here; a formal weighted scorecard would restate chains C2-C4's conclusions in a different format without adding evidence.

**What it ruled out:** Treating this as a selection decision; it is a claim-verification task, so the trade-off procedure's trigger condition (two or more viable options surviving as a live choice) does not fire, and the procedure is recorded as not applicable in the Techniques not applied block (Appendix).

### Dead End: Applying the fishbone procedure to the assumption space

**What was tried:** Using the fishbone (breadth-first, categorical) brainstorming technique to enumerate the assumption space in Phase 2.

**Why abandoned:** The assumption space here is a bounded, well-structured physics-plus-economics decomposition with a small number of clearly identifiable load-bearing variables (temperatures, efficiency figures, cost figures) — not a multi-causal diagnostic problem ("why does X keep happening") where intuition cannot enumerate the cause space confidently. Direct enumeration in the Assumptions Table (Section 2) was tractable without a categorical brainstorm.

**What it ruled out:** A fishbone pass would not have surfaced assumptions beyond those already in Section 2; recorded as not applicable in the Techniques not applied block (Appendix).

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Reject the claim as stated. An 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically unreachable for a heat engine spanning 290-565°C under any plausible reading of that temperature pair, and the cost-competitiveness comparison to a same-capacity Li-ion BESS fails independently, driven by small-scale power-block diseconomies and the efficiency shortfall itself (chain C1, chain C4).

**Key insight:** The 85% figure is not an ambitious-but-missed engineering target — it exceeds the thermodynamic ceiling itself (62.6-64.4% under the most generous ambient-sink reading, 32.8% under a literal two-tank-as-sink reading), so no engineering improvement at any scale closes that gap for a power-to-power architecture (chain C1). The number most plausibly originates from a real but different metric: the most credible named real-world comparator, Malta Inc., reports 85-95% only as a combined heat-and-power (cogeneration) figure, not an electricity-to-electricity one — exactly the S2 conflation this analysis flagged in Section 1 (chain C3).

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** Molten-salt thermal storage has two genuine, non-fabricated advantages over Li-ion: a cheap storage medium per kWh, and a much longer calendar/mechanical life (20-30 years vs. Li-ion's cycle-limited 10-15 years). Neither advantage is large enough to reverse the cost-competitiveness verdict at 5 MWh / multi-hour scale, because the power-conversion equipment cost and the efficiency-driven charging-energy cost dominate at this scale; both advantages become decisive only at much larger scale and longer duration than the claim describes (chain C4).

**Sub-claim verdicts:**

| Sub-claim | Verdict | Chain |
|---|---|---|
| S1 — >85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency | False — exceeds the Carnot ceiling, not merely unlikely | C1 |
| S2 — "electricity into heat and back" means power-to-power | True as read; this is what makes S1 fail rather than merely underperform | C1, C3 |
| S3 — 5 MWh scale doesn't change the physics | False — small power-block turbomachinery and adverse surface/volume scaling plausibly cut real efficiency to ~18-25%, below even utility-scale reference figures | C2 |
| S4 — cost-competitive with same-capacity Li-ion | False, with one unresolved caveat (A-13) — power-block diseconomies of scale plus the efficiency penalty raise levelized cost on both the capital and operating-energy components, but the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is unspecified | C4 |

**What would change this conclusion:** Restricting the claim to power-to-heat delivery (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85-90% is routine and commercially demonstrated (chain C3); or restricting the power-to-power/cost comparison to utility scale (100+ MWh, long duration), where the best credible architecture (Malta's projected 55-60%) at least becomes capex-structurally relevant against large Li-ion installations — though still well under the claimed 85% (chains C1, C4). Neither restatement matches the claim as written, which specifies a 5 MWh electrical nameplate compared directly against a same-capacity Li-ion BESS.

**Confidence:** MEDIUM overall, but with an internal split that matters: the core physics falsification of S1 (chain C1) is **HIGH** confidence and sufficient on its own to reject the claim as stated — it rests only on unsuffixed, physical-law ground truths with no live rival. The magnitude estimates for S3 (chain C2, MEDIUM) and the real-world corroboration for S2/S3 (chain C3, MEDIUM) and the cost-competitiveness verdict for S4 (chain C4, MEDIUM) all carry an unverified-input discount — primarily GT-8?, GT-9?, GT-10?, and GT-11?, none of which were confirmed against a primary source in this session (three WebFetch attempts failed: a 404 on Malta's own data sheet, a 403 on the Li-ion efficiency field-data article, and a DNS failure on NREL's SolarPACES database). The Phase 5 adversarial (inversion) pass surfaced one additional, specifically cost-side caveat not previously tracked: chain C4's final hop rests on **A-13** (unverified) — that the claim's implied Li-ion comparator is a normal, representative same-duration/power-rating system — which this analysis cannot verify because the claim specifies no comparator configuration; this caveat applies only to S4 and does not touch S1's physics falsification. What would raise the overall band to HIGH: a primary, itemized capex bill-of-materials for a ~1 MWe-class molten-salt power block; a primary (not WebSearch-summarized) performance report for an operating CSP plant's power-block efficiency; either a working Malta data-sheet link or an independent audit of Malta's 55-60%/85-95% figures; and a source specifying the claim's intended Li-ion comparator (A-13). None of these would overturn the headline verdict (C1 alone is already sufficient and HIGH-confidence) — they would only sharpen the magnitude of S3's and the certainty of S4's secondary conclusions.

## Verdict: Reject the claim

**The 85% figure isn't an ambitious engineering target that falls short — it's thermodynamically impossible.**

### The core falsification (high confidence)

The claim describes a heat engine cycling between 290°C (563 K) and 565°C (838 K). Any such engine is bounded by the Carnot limit:

η ≤ 1 − T_cold/T_hot

- **Literal reading** (290°C as the actual sink, i.e. the cold tank is the heat-rejection reservoir): η ≤ 1 − 563.15/838.15 = **32.8%**
- **Generous reading** (true ambient condenser sink, ~25–40°C, with 290°C just describing the cold *tank* in the storage loop, not the engine's cold reservoir): η ≤ **62.6–64.4%**

Either way, 85% sits far above the *ideal, lossless* ceiling — before you even subtract real turbine, heat-exchanger, pump, and parasitic losses. No engineering improvement at any price point closes that gap for a power-to-power device. This is a Second Law violation, not an underperformance.

### Where "85%" likely actually comes from

The real-world reference points (Malta Inc., Siemens Gamesa ETES) cluster around **45–60%** electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency — consistent with the Carnot math above. The one place "85–95%" shows up in industry literature is as a **cogeneration figure** (electricity + usable delivered process heat combined), not an electricity-to-electricity number. The claim's own wording ("heat and back") specifies the power-to-power case, so this is almost certainly a terminology conflation — power-to-heat storage is routinely >85–90%, but that's a different quantity than what's claimed.

### Scale makes it worse, not better

5 MWh implies a power block on the order of ~1 MWe — two orders of magnitude below the 50–100+ MWe utility-scale CSP plants that the ~38–40% discharge-efficiency figures come from. Small turbines/ORC units run far less efficiently, and a small tank has a worse surface-to-volume ratio plus standing trace-heating parasitic load (nitrate salt freezes near 220°C and must be kept hot continuously). Net estimate for a 5 MWh system: **~18–25% real-world round-trip efficiency**, not 85%.

### Cost-competitiveness fails independently

- Li-ion AC-AC round-trip efficiency: ~85–92% (established, not in dispute)
- Thermal system at this scale: ~18–25%

That means the thermal system must buy **roughly 3–5x more input electricity** for the same delivered output, on top of small-scale power-block hardware (turbine/generator/controls) costing proportionally much more per kW than at utility scale, since that equipment doesn't shrink economically. Thermal storage's genuine advantages — cheap storage medium per kWh, 20–30 year tank/salt life vs. Li-ion's 10–15 year cycle life — are real but only become decisive at much larger scale and longer duration than 5 MWh, not enough to offset this gap here.

### Bottom line

| Sub-claim | Verdict |
|---|---|
| >85% round-trip efficiency | **False** — exceeds the Carnot ceiling itself |
| 5 MWh scale doesn't change the physics | **False** — small-scale penalties drag real efficiency to ~18–25% |
| Cost-competitive with same-capacity Li-ion | **False** — efficiency penalty + power-block diseconomies of scale both cut against it |

The claim would become defensible only if restated as either (a) a power-to-*heat* delivery claim (no reconversion to electricity) at any scale, where >85% is routine, or (b) a utility-scale (100+ MWh), long-duration comparison, where the best credible real architecture tops out around 55–60% — still short of 85%, but at least cost-structurally relevant.

Full derivation (Carnot math, ground-truth sourcing, confidence bands, and figures) is saved at `.first-principles/report-20261015T032239Z.md` and `.pdf` in the working directory if you want to dig into the sourcing weak points (several citations hit dead links/403s and are flagged as unverified-but-not-load-bearing).
